gh-choose-life.title: The Kitchen Table Ballot
gh-choose-life.body: Every morning at six, Walter Price sat down at the same scratched kitchen table with two things in front of him: his phone and his worn Bible. He had noticed, the winter his first child was born, that whichever one he picked up first quietly decided the rest of his day. The phone meant news, worry, and a short temper by breakfast. The open Bible meant a slower heart and a gentler voice. So he made it a rule: the Word first, before anything else got a vote. His children grew up padding into the kitchen in their socks and finding their father already reading, a mug of coffee going cold beside him. They did not think much of it. It was simply what mornings looked like. Then they started pulling up chairs. His daughter Bess asked questions. His son Danny pretended he was not listening and listened anyway. Years later Walter drove three hours to visit Danny, now a father himself, and arrived before dawn. The porch light was on. Through the kitchen window he saw his son at a table of his own, Bible open, phone face down at the far edge, and a small boy in pajamas climbing up into the chair beside him. Walter stood in the cold yard a long minute without knocking. He had made that choice in a quiet kitchen thirty years before, mostly on mornings when he did not feel like it. He had never once preached it. And here it was, still being chosen, one table further down the line.

gh-choose-life.title: The Door That Stopped Slamming
gh-choose-life.body: Harlan Brooks came from a long line of slammed doors. His father had a temper that filled a house like smoke, and Harlan had carried it out of that house into his own. He never struck anyone, but he shouted, he sulked for days, and he slammed doors hard enough to rattle the dishes. His son learned it too, the way boys learn everything, by watching. One Sunday afternoon Harlan sat on his son's porch and watched his six-year-old grandson, Eli, lose a board game, sweep the pieces onto the floor, stomp inside, and slam the screen door so hard it bounced. Eli's father yelled after him. Harlan felt something go cold in his chest. He was not looking at a little boy's tantrum. He was looking at his own father, at himself, and at a choice that had been handed down unexamined for three generations. That evening Harlan did what no man in his family had ever done. He gathered his son and grandson at the table and said, plainly, that the temper in their family was wrong, that it had started long before them, and that it had to stop with him. He asked their forgiveness for every door he had ever slammed. Then he asked Yahweh for help, out loud, with his voice shaking. It took him years to learn to walk away and breathe and pray before he spoke. He failed sometimes and owned it each time. But one summer Eli, now ten, lost a ballgame, walked out to the porch, sat beside his grandfather, and said he was angry. Then he closed the door behind him. Gently.

gh-obedience-blessing.title: The Cobbler Who Stopped Chasing
gh-obedience-blessing.body: Amos Reed fixed shoes in a narrow shop between a bakery and a bank, and for years he spent more time chasing customers than mending soles. He printed coupons. He stood on the sidewalk waving a sign. He promised repairs by Tuesday that he knew could not be ready until Friday, because a promise brought people in the door. And still the bell over his door hardly rang. One rainy evening, sweeping up, Amos asked Yahweh a plain question: what would You have me do? The answer that settled in his heart was not about customers at all. Tell the truth. Do the work well. Rest on the Lord's day. Treat every pair of shoes as if it belonged to a friend. So he did. He told people Friday when it would be Friday. He stitched heels the slow, right way. He closed his shop on Sundays and went to church with his sister. He stopped waving the sign and started praying for the people whose boots sat on his shelf. Nothing happened for a while. Then a nurse told a teacher, who told a mail carrier, who told her whole route, that there was a cobbler on Main Street who never lied to you. A bride came looking for him to save her grandmother's wedding shoes. A farmer drove in from the next county. By spring there was a line on Saturday mornings, and the bell rang so often his sister tied a ribbon on it to soften the sound. Amos laughed when he noticed it. He had stopped chasing, and the work had come looking for him.

gh-obedience-blessing.title: The Promotion She Ran After
gh-obedience-blessing.body: Delia Marsh wanted the regional manager job more than she had ever wanted anything. So she ran after it. She stayed at the office past nine every night. She took credit for a project her coworker Ruth had carried. She rounded the quarterly numbers a little higher than they really were, telling herself everyone did it. She missed her daughter's spring concert, and then the next one. The job went to someone else. Driving home that night she sat a long time in her dark driveway, her hands still on the wheel, and saw with sudden clearness what she had become while chasing it. She went inside and found her daughter asleep with the concert program still on her pillow. Delia began, slowly, to turn. The next morning she told her supervisor the truth about the numbers. She told Ruth the truth about the project and asked her forgiveness. She started leaving at six so she could eat supper with her family, and she began reading the Word at the table each morning before she read her email. She stopped asking how to get ahead and started asking how to do right. Her pay did not change for two years. She did not mind as much as she expected. Then on a quiet Saturday, while she was planting tomatoes with her daughter, her phone rang. It was the woman who had gotten the manager job, now moving to another city. She wanted to know if Delia would take her place. The company needed someone, she said, that everyone could trust. Delia set down her trowel. She had not been looking. It had come looking for her.

gh-passover-blood.title: The Smallest House on Cedar Lane
gh-passover-blood.body: Lily Hart lived in the smallest house on Cedar Lane, and she knew it. The paint was peeling, the porch sagged, and the front door had a dent from the time her brother kicked a ball too hard. All her friends lived in bigger, newer houses with stone walls and shiny doors. One spring evening Lily found her father on a stepladder, painting the frame around their front door a fresh coat of white. She asked why he bothered when the whole house needed fixing. He climbed down, wiped his hands, and sat with her on the step. Every spring, he said, when he painted this doorframe, he prayed for everyone who slept inside. Not because the frame was special. It was just a reminder. Their family was not safe because their house was strong. A strong house can still be shaken. They were safe because they had put themselves under Jesus, the Lamb of Yahweh, and His Blood covers the people who trust Him, whether they sleep in a palace or a shack. Lily thought about that for a long time. That summer a terrible storm blew through town and the power went out on every street. Lily's friend Grace came over, shaking, because the thunder sounded louder in her big house than it ever had. The two girls sat on the sagging porch under a blanket while Lily's father prayed. Grace said she had never felt so safe. Lily looked up at the plain white doorframe and smiled. She knew it was not the door doing it.

gh-passover-blood.title: Good Enough Doorframes
gh-passover-blood.body: For fifty years Franklin Moss had been the most dependable man at Bethel Church. He had unlocked the doors every Sunday, fixed the furnace, counted the offering, and visited every shut-in on the list. People said there was no better man in the county. So it surprised his granddaughter Joy when she found him in his hospital bed, near the end, afraid. She pulled her chair close and asked what was wrong. He told her, in a voice she had never heard from him, that he did not know if he had done enough. He kept counting his years of service like coins and coming up short. He remembered every harsh word, every Sunday he had served with a proud heart. What if the doorframe was not good enough? Joy held his rough hand. She reminded him of a sermon he himself had loved, about the night the families painted the Blood on their doors. The judgment had not passed over the houses with the best carpentry. It had passed over the houses with the Blood on them. His fifty years were a gift of love, she said, but they had never been his covering. Jesus was. Franklin was quiet for a long time. Then, with tears running into his gray whiskers, he prayed like a child. He told Yahweh he had been trusting his own doorframe, and he was sorry, and he put himself, house and all, under the Blood of the Lamb and nothing else. When Joy came back the next morning, the fear was gone from his face. He slept that night like a man with nothing left to prove.

gh-house-serve.title: The Night We Said It Out Loud
gh-house-serve.body: Marcus Bell called a family meeting on a Tuesday night, which made his three kids certain someone was in trouble. Instead he set a plate of cookies on the table and said he had realized something. Their family had never actually decided who they served. They went to church most Sundays. They prayed before supper, mostly. But nobody had ever said it out loud. So Marcus said it. He told them that as long as he was the father of this house, their family would serve Yahweh. Then he asked what that ought to look like on a regular Tuesday. The kids had ideas. Ten minutes of reading the Word after supper. A jar on the counter for giving. Saying sorry before bed, not the next week. His wife wrote it all on an index card and taped it to the fridge. A month later a coach called about a travel soccer team that played every Sunday morning. Their oldest, Ava, loved soccer more than anything. Marcus braced for a long, painful argument. But Ava just looked at the index card on the fridge and sighed. She said she guessed that was already decided, wasn't it, and asked if there was a Saturday league instead. There was. It took four minutes. Marcus noticed that week how many small choices had gotten easier since the meeting. What to watch, where to spend, how to speak. They had stopped fighting the same battles every day, because the biggest question had already been answered, out loud, at the kitchen table, over a plate of cookies.

gh-house-serve.title: The Undeclared House
gh-house-serve.body: Joanna Cruz always assumed her children would simply turn out like her. She loved Yahweh. Her husband did too, in a quiet way. They never talked about it much at home, because they thought it would just soak in. Then one autumn she looked up and realized her two teenagers belonged to everything but Him. Their opinions came from their phones. Their heroes were strangers. Their weekends were full, and church was the first thing to go whenever anything else came up. When she tried to talk about faith at dinner, they rolled their eyes as if she had started speaking a foreign language. One night she sat alone in the dark living room and wept. Her house had a direction after all. It was just not one she had chosen. No one had pointed it, so the world had pointed it for them. The next Sunday afternoon she gathered the family and did the hardest thing she had ever done. She told her children she had failed them. She had never said out loud whom this house served, and she was saying it now: this house belonged to the Lord. She did not lecture. She asked their forgiveness. Then she and her husband began building, plainly and stubbornly. Supper together four nights a week. Phones in a basket at the door. Prayer, even when it was awkward. Serving at the food pantry as a family on the first Saturday of every month. The eye-rolling did not stop right away. But a year later her son asked, quietly, if he could be the one to pray that night. Joanna had to leave the table for a minute before she could answer.

gh-joy-untakeable.title: What the Rain Could Not Take
gh-joy-untakeable.body: Mr. Okafor was the crossing guard at Lincoln Elementary, and every child in the school knew two things about him. He wore a bright orange vest, and he was always glad. He hummed while he held up his stop sign. He greeted every child by name. A group of fourth graders, led by a boy named Wesley, decided one spring to find out what could make him stop. They watched him on a day of pouring rain, water dripping off his cap. Still humming. They watched him the morning a driver honked and shouted at him for making her wait. He waved and wished her a good day. They watched him the week his old car broke down and he had to walk two miles to work. He arrived humming. Finally Wesley could not stand it anymore and simply asked him. How could anybody be that happy all the time? Mr. Okafor laughed his big laugh. He said he was not happy all the time. Rain was cold, and rude people stung, and walking two miles in old shoes made his feet hurt. But happy was not the same as joy. His joy came from Yahweh, who had loved him since before he was born, and none of those things had given it to him. So none of those things could take it away. That was why he had strength for the corner every morning. Wesley thought about that all the way across the street. The next day it rained again. He walked to school without his hood, humming, just to see if it worked.

gh-joy-untakeable.title: What the Layoff Could Not Repossess
gh-joy-untakeable.body: Benjamin Hale had been a manager at the plant for nineteen years when the letter came. The company was closing his department. He packed his desk into a single cardboard box and drove home, and for weeks afterward he hardly left the couch. He was not lazy. He was empty. He sat by the window watching the mailbox, and when his wife Clara asked him to come to church, he said he did not have the strength. One evening Clara sat beside him and asked a quiet question. Where had his joy been coming from? Benjamin started to answer and stopped. The title. The parking spot with his name on it. The men who came to him for answers. The paycheck that made him feel like a good provider. All of it had been given to him by the plant, and so the plant had been able to take it back. He had been drawing his strength from something that could be repossessed. That night Benjamin knelt by the couch for the first time in years. He told Yahweh he had been living on the wrong supply. He asked for the joy that came from Him and could not be taken by any company or any letter. Nothing outside changed for a while. But something inside did. He started getting up early again. He fixed the church's leaking roof with two other men from the plant. He sent out applications without dreading each one. When a new job came in the fall, it paid less than the old one. Benjamin took it gladly. His joy had not been in the paycheck. It never would be again.

gh-joy-three-days.title: Three Days at the Corner Diner
gh-joy-three-days.body: Rosa worked the breakfast shift at the corner diner, and she had a habit her coworkers teased her about. Before every shift she sat in her car for one minute and did the same four things. She told Yahweh honestly how she felt. She reminded herself where her joy came from. She picked one thing to be thankful for and one person to bless. Then she went inside. On Monday everything went wrong. She dropped a tray of eggs, a customer yelled about his coffee, and her bus was late. In the car she said it plainly: Lord, today is hard. Then she thanked Him that her daughter's fever had broken, and she slipped an extra muffin to the dishwasher, who looked worn out. She made it through the shift with strength she did not have at six. On Wednesday nothing happened at all. It was a gray, ordinary day, the kind that slides by without anyone noticing. Rosa almost skipped her minute. Then she did it anyway, thanking Him for the day just because He had made it, and she spent her break helping the new waitress learn the register. On Friday a man left her a fifty-dollar tip on a twelve-dollar check. Rosa sat in her car afterward laughing and told Yahweh thank You, because she knew where it came from. Then she bought lunch for the cook. Her friend Dina asked how she stayed steady on every kind of day. Rosa said the first line was different every morning. The last line never was.

gh-joy-three-days.title: Grandpa's Ledger
gh-joy-three-days.body: After Silas Ward died, his grandson Tyler found a stack of small green ledgers in the farmhouse desk. He had expected crop numbers. Instead each page was a single day, written in his grandfather's careful pencil, and every page had the same four lines. The first line was how the day really was. The second was where his joy came from. The third was what he had done about it. The fourth was always the same. Tyler turned to the summer of the hailstorm, the year the whole wheat crop was lost. The first line said: Hail took the wheat. I sat in the truck and cried. The second line said: My joy is in the Lord, not the wheat. The third said: Counted what is left. House, wife, boys, the well. Took a pie to the Larsons, they lost more than us. And the fourth line said what it said on every page: Strength for tomorrow. His, not mine. Tyler turned to an ordinary Tuesday. First line: Nothing much. Fixed fence. Same second line, a small kindness on the third, the same fourth. He turned to the day Tyler's own father was born. First line: A son! Best day of my life. Second line: This joy is from Him too. Do not let it become the source. Third: Thanked Him first. Gave the church the first calf. And the fourth, the same. Tyler sat at the desk until dark. He had been told his grandfather was the steadiest man in the valley. Now he could see exactly how it was done, one honest page at a time.

gh-genesis-holds-the-whole-plan.title: The Club With One Book
gh-genesis-holds-the-whole-plan.body: When the printer at Grace Chapel broke, Mr. Hollis had only one thing left to hand out to his Wednesday Bible club: a stack of booklets that held just the book of Genesis. The kids grumbled. They wanted the stories about Jesus. Mr. Hollis smiled and said he would make them a deal. If they could not find the whole rescue plan inside this one book, he would buy pizza. They spent six Wednesdays hunting, and they kept a list on the whiteboard. Page one: Yahweh creating, His Spirit moving over the waters, His Word speaking the light into being. A girl named Priya counted and wrote down three. Chapter one again: Yahweh speaking of Himself as us. Chapter three: after the man and woman did wrong, He came looking for them before He did anything else, and in the very sentence against the serpent He promised a Child who would crush its head. Then He made them clothes from an animal, which meant something had to die to cover them. A boy named Caleb wrote that one in big letters. Later came Abram, who simply believed, and it was counted as righteousness. And last came the mountain, where a father trusted Yahweh to provide a lamb in his son's place, and He did. On the sixth Wednesday the board was full. The kids sat staring at it. Priya said it was like the whole story of Jesus was hiding in the first book, waiting. Mr. Hollis said it was not hiding. It had been there all along. He bought the pizza anyway.

gh-genesis-holds-the-whole-plan.title: The Coat in the Garden
gh-genesis-holds-the-whole-plan.body: Reuben Stone had not spoken to his brother Aaron in four years, ever since he had quietly moved money out of their shared business and let the company fail. He told himself it had been necessary. He told himself many things. But he could not go to his brother, and he could not stop hiding. One sleepless night he opened a Bible for the first time in decades and started at the beginning, because that was where you started. He read slowly through the garden and the fall. He had expected to find Yahweh angry and cold. What he found stopped him. After the man and woman disobeyed and hid among the trees, Yahweh came looking for them. He called for them. He asked where they were, though He knew. Before any sentence fell, He went seeking. Then, in the middle of the hardest chapter, He promised a Rescuer. And before He sent them out of the garden, He made coverings from animal skins and put the coats on them Himself. Reuben sat back in his chair. Something had died so they could be covered. The One they had wronged had made the covering with His own hands. He read on into the story of Abram, who did nothing but believe and was counted righteous. Reuben closed the book at dawn and prayed for the first time since he was a boy, and he received what he could not earn. Then he drove two hours to Aaron's house with a check and a confession. Aaron opened the door, listened in silence, and then pulled his brother inside.

gh-humble-heal.title: The Church That Started With Itself
gh-humble-heal.body: The little church on Mill Street loved to talk about how bad the town had gotten. The empty storefronts, the trash in the vacant lot, the teenagers with nowhere to go. Every Wednesday prayer meeting turned into a complaint meeting. Then one night old Mrs. Pruitt, who had not said a word in months, stood up with her cane. She said she was tired of praying about everybody else's sins. She thought maybe Yahweh was waiting on them first. The room went very quiet. Then Mrs. Pruitt confessed that she had gossiped about the pastor's wife for two years, and she asked her forgiveness right there. The pastor's wife cried and hugged her. Mr. Dunn admitted he had not spoken to the Garcia family since an argument over the parking lot. One by one, people humbled themselves. They began meeting early on Saturdays just to pray and to read the Word together. They turned from grudges they had kept for years. That spring Mr. Dunn and Mr. Garcia, of all people, decided together to clean up the vacant lot behind the church. The teenagers came to watch, then to help. By summer it was a garden with tomatoes and sunflowers and a basketball hoop on the far end. The hardware store owner donated a bench. A neighbor who had never set foot in the church came to water the beans. Nobody had marched or demanded anything of the town. The healing had started on the inside of one small church, and the ground around it seemed to have noticed.

gh-humble-heal.title: The Creek Between the Brothers
gh-humble-heal.body: The Talbot brothers had farmed side by side for thirty years until a fight over their late father's will split the land in two. After that they did not speak. The creek that ran between their fields got clogged with branches and silt, and since each brother believed the other should clear it, neither did. Every spring the water backed up and flooded the low ground. Every summer the crops on both sides came in thinner. Their children stopped visiting. The whole valley knew the Talbot land was sick. One wet April, Owen Talbot stood at the edge of his drowned field and finally saw the truth. The creek was not the real problem. His pride was. He had been praying for rain to stop and crops to grow, but he had never once prayed about his own heart. He went home and knelt by his bed. He confessed his bitterness to Yahweh plainly and asked Him to search him. He sought the Lord for a week, morning and night, and the Lord did not let him off easy. On the eighth day Owen walked across the muddy field with two shovels. His brother Ezra saw him coming and stood up from his porch, ready for a fight. Owen held out a shovel and said he had been wrong, and he was sorry. Ezra stared at him for a long moment. Then he took the shovel. They worked until dark clearing the creek together, not saying much. The water ran free that night for the first time in years. By June both sides of the creek were green.

gh-told-before-he-came.title: The Extra Plate
gh-told-before-he-came.body: On Saturday night, while Martha Kemp was praying for the week ahead, a small, clear thought settled in her heart. Set an extra plate tomorrow. Someone is coming. It was so plain and so specific that she smiled and told Yahweh she would. The next morning her family teased her as she laid out seven plates for a family of six. Her husband asked who she had invited. Nobody, she said. She just knew. At church that morning she noticed a young man sitting alone in the back row, holding his coffee like he was not sure he was allowed to have it. He wore a jacket too thin for the weather. When the service ended he headed straight for the door, and Martha felt the thought again, as clear as the night before. That one. She caught up with him on the steps and asked if he had plans for lunch. His name was Daniel. He had moved to town two weeks earlier for a job at the warehouse, and he did not know a single soul. He had almost not come to church at all. He sat down at the Kemp table in front of the seventh plate and looked at it for a moment. Martha's youngest asked him, with her mouth full, whether he knew Mama had set his plate before she ever met him. Daniel laughed and then went quiet. Over the next year he came to lunch nearly every Sunday. The family stopped teasing Martha about her extra plate. They had learned to pay attention when she set one.

gh-told-before-he-came.title: The Night Before the Knock
gh-told-before-he-came.body: Walter Lane had been retired from preaching for six years, and on Thursdays he went fishing. But on Wednesday night, as he prayed in his old armchair, an impression came so strongly that he set down his reading glasses. Stay home tomorrow. Someone will come. Be ready to listen. He argued with it a little. Then he put his fishing pole back in the closet. Thursday crawled by. He made coffee. He read. He waited. By late afternoon he was beginning to feel foolish. Then, just as the sun went low, there was a knock at the door. A young man stood on the porch, maybe twenty-five, his eyes red and his shoulders bent. His name was Caleb. He said he did not know why he had come. He had driven past the little house a hundred times, and today he had simply stopped. His marriage was coming apart, he had lost his job, and he had decided he was finished with church and finished with hoping. Walter looked at him, and the quiet word from the night before came back with great weight. This was the one. He had been told the day before. Walter did not rush him. He opened the door wide, sat Caleb at the kitchen table, poured coffee, and listened for three hours. He prayed with him, and the next morning he drove him to meet a counselor from his old church. A year later Caleb and his wife renewed their vows in that church. Walter sat in the front row. He had given up one day of fishing, and he had been ready when the knock came.

gh-provider-prepared.title: The Farmer Who Was Expecting Them
gh-provider-prepared.body: When the Reyes family felt Yahweh calling them to the little town of Harlow, everything about it looked foolish on paper. Miguel had been offered a teaching job at the struggling school there, but the pay was small, and they had found nowhere to live. Their friends asked how they could pack up three kids and a dog without a house lined up. Miguel and his wife Ana only said they believed they were supposed to go, and they would trust Him for the rest. They drove in on a Friday evening with the car full and no idea where they would sleep that night. They stopped at the only diner in town. An old farmer in overalls at the counter turned around on his stool and asked, before they had even ordered, if they were the new teacher's family. Miguel said they were. The farmer's name was Mr. Lindqvist. For months, he told them, he had been praying for that school, which could not keep a teacher. One morning last winter, while he was praying, he had felt the Lord tell him plainly to fix up the old cottage behind his barn, because a teacher's family was coming and would need a place. So he had. New roof, new stove, fresh paint. It had been sitting empty and ready since March. Ana put her hand over her mouth. The kids ran ahead to see it. That night the Reyes family slept under a new roof in a cottage that had been waiting for them long before they ever said yes.

gh-provider-prepared.title: Arise and Go
gh-provider-prepared.body: Grace Moreno was a young nurse who believed Yahweh had told her to move to the city and serve at a free clinic in its poorest neighborhood. The clinic could pay her almost nothing. She had no apartment and no friends there. Her mother wept and asked her to wait until she could see how she would live. Grace said she could not see it. She only knew she had been told to go. Across the city, a widow named Hannah Price lived alone in a narrow row house with an empty spare room and a nearly empty pantry. Her husband had died two winters before. She was lonely, and the money was running out, and some nights she wondered what use she was to anyone. One evening as she prayed, a strong impression came over her: make up the spare room. Someone is coming who will need it, and you will need her too. Hannah did not understand, but she washed the sheets and set a lamp on the dresser. Two weeks later Grace stood in the clinic office asking where she might find a cheap room, and the receptionist, who went to church with Hannah, wrote down an address. When Hannah opened her door, she looked at the young woman with her one suitcase and began to cry. She had been expecting her. Grace's small paycheck covered the groceries that Hannah could not. Hannah's spare room gave Grace a home. For three years they kept each other. Neither had seen the other end of the road when she obeyed. Yahweh had been arranging both ends at once.

gh-only-he-knows-the-heart.title: The Boy Who Thought His Thoughts Were Loud
gh-only-he-knows-the-heart.body: Theo was nine, and he had a secret fear. Somebody at camp had told him that the enemy could hear everything you think, every second, and Theo could not stop worrying about it. At night he lay awake trying not to think anything at all, which only made his thoughts louder. Finally he told his grandmother, while they were shelling peas on her back porch. She set down her bowl and pointed to the wooden fence at the edge of her yard. If a stranger stood out there by the fence, she asked, what could he see? Theo thought. He could see what you were doing. Where you went. Who came over. He could hear you if you yelled. Could he see inside the house? Theo shook his head. That, said his grandmother, is all the adversary can do: stand at the fence, see what you look at, hear what you say, and then guess. But that watcher cannot see your heart. Only Yahweh knows the heart, every heart in the whole world, because He made them. And He is not a stranger at the fence. He is the Father who loves you and lives inside the house with you. Theo let out a long breath. His grandmother told him to be careful with the outside things, what he watched and what he said and who he spent time with, and to bring the inside things straight to Yahweh, because He already knew them and loved him anyway. That night Theo told the Lord everything on his mind. Then he fell asleep.

gh-only-he-knows-the-heart.title: Only Guessing
gh-only-he-knows-the-heart.body: After Miriam Hayes lost her temper with her teenage son and said things she could never take back, the accusing thoughts would not leave her alone. You are a terrible mother. Everyone can see it. You will always be this way. They seemed to know her so well that she began to believe the voice could see straight into her. She stopped going to her small group. She stopped praying, because she felt watched and judged even there. One Sunday her friend Lorraine found her sitting alone in her car in the church parking lot. Miriam told her everything. Lorraine listened and then said something Miriam had never considered. The accuser only watches from the outside, seeing her slammed door, her slumped shoulders, her missed meetings, and guessing at the rest. The accuser does not know the heart. Only Yahweh searches the heart, and He is not guessing. He knows exactly what is in her, the sin and the sorrow both, and He is the One who offers to cleanse it. Miriam sat very still. She had been listening to a watcher as though he were Yahweh. That night she knelt by her bed and opened her whole heart to the only One who could truly see it. She confessed her anger, all of it, and asked Him to search the rest. Then she went to her son's room and asked his forgiveness. She guarded the outside too, more carefully than before: her words, her evenings, her friends. The accusing thoughts still came sometimes. But now she knew they were only guessing, and she knew who actually knew.

gh-sons-of-god-and-giants.title: The Question About Giants
gh-sons-of-god-and-giants.body: Owen was eleven, and he had saved up his question all week. When Mrs. Abbott finished the Sunday school lesson, his hand shot up. Were there really giants in the Bible? A few kids laughed. Mrs. Abbott did not. She said it was a good question and that the Word answers it best when you let the Word explain itself. So they opened their Bibles to Genesis 6 and read it slowly together. Then Owen asked who the strange sons in the second verse were. Instead of telling them what people argue about, Mrs. Abbott had them turn to the book of Job, where the very same name is used for heavenly beings who stand before Yahweh. The class leaned in. The Word was explaining its own words. She showed them that giants were there before the great flood and also after it, because years later the spies Moses sent into the promised land came back trembling about them. They said they had felt as small as bugs. A girl named Hope asked if that meant they should be scared. Mrs. Abbott smiled and turned a few pages to a man named Caleb, one of those same spies. He was not scared at all. He trusted Yahweh, and when he was eighty-five years old he asked for the very hill country where the giants lived, and he took it. Then she reminded them of the promise in Genesis 3, that the Seed of the woman would crush the serpent. That Seed is Jesus, she said, and He already won. Owen went home thinking giants were real, and that they were not nearly as big as Yahweh.

gh-sons-of-god-and-giants.title: Neither Spooked Nor Explaining Away
gh-sons-of-god-and-giants.body: Ezra Collins was nineteen, home from college for the summer, and he had stopped sleeping well. Late at night he had started watching long videos about ancient giants and secret powers, and each one was darker and stranger than the last. Some claimed the old stories proved that frightening forces secretly ran the world. Others laughed that the whole thing was a fairy tale. Ezra did not know which voice to believe, and the not knowing had turned into a heavy fear. One night his grandfather, a quiet farmer who rarely said much, found him awake at the kitchen table at two in the morning. Ezra told him what he had been watching. His grandfather did not scold him. He went and got his old Bible and sat down beside him under the lamp. They read Genesis 6 together, slowly, as it was written. Then his grandfather turned to Job and showed him how the Word itself used that very same name for heavenly beings who stood before Yahweh, and who sang when He laid the foundations of the earth. The account was real, his grandfather said. The war over the human line was old and serious. But the Word did not tell it to frighten anyone, and it did not leave the story there. He turned back to the third chapter and laid his weathered finger on the promise of the Seed who would crush the serpent's head. That promise had been kept in Jesus. Ezra read it three times. Then he closed the laptop, and he slept, for the first time in weeks, like someone standing in a safe place.

gh-made-in-his-image.title: The Mark on the Bottom of the Bowl
gh-made-in-his-image.body: Clara's bowl came out of the kiln lopsided. One side sloped lower than the other, and there was a lumpy thumbprint near the rim. Every other bowl in the pottery class looked smooth and even. Clara slid hers behind her back and wished she could throw it away. Mrs. Dahl, the potter who taught the class, noticed and held out her hand. Clara gave it to her slowly. Mrs. Dahl did not look at the lopsided side at all. She turned the bowl over and pointed to the bottom, where Clara had scratched her initials into the wet clay a week before. Whose mark is this, she asked. Clara said it was hers. Mrs. Dahl said that was why the bowl mattered. Not because it was perfect, but because of who made it. She told Clara that every person was the same way. Yahweh made each one in His own image, on purpose, with care, and His mark was on them. Nobody had to earn being worth something. They only had to find out who had made them. Clara carried the bowl home on her lap. At school that week she noticed a boy named Simon who got teased for his stutter. Kids called him names. Clara thought about the mark on the bottom of her bowl, and she sat down next to him at lunch. If Yahweh had made Simon too, she figured, then Simon had the same kind of mark she did, whether anyone could see it or not. Her lopsided bowl still sits on her desk. She keeps pencils in it, and she likes it very much.

gh-made-in-his-image.title: The Man Who Built Himself
gh-made-in-his-image.body: Graham Lowe had spent his whole life building a self worth admiring. He had been a star athlete, then a top salesman, then the owner of three restaurants. Each time one thing faded, he reinvented himself into something new and more impressive, and he wore each new version like a coat. He never asked who he actually was. He only asked who people thought he was. Then in one year the restaurants failed, his knee gave out, and the friends who had loved the successful Graham stopped calling. He sat in a rented room with nothing left to build with, and he did not know what was underneath. One night, unable to sleep, he picked up a Bible his mother had given him decades before and opened it at the very beginning. He read about the very first man and woman, made by Yahweh in His own image, on purpose. He read the page again, slowly, and something in him broke open. His worth had never been the athlete or the salesman or the owner. It had been given to him by his Maker before he ever did a single thing. Every identity he had built had to be defended because he had built it. This one had simply been received. Graham did not become someone new overnight. But he stopped performing. He took a job as a line cook, and he began to treat the dishwashers and busboys the way he had once treated only important customers, because they bore the same image he did. A young cook named Luis asked him once why he was so kind to everybody. Graham told him he had finally found out who made them both.

gh-el-elyon-possessor.title: Whose Tree Is It
gh-el-elyon-possessor.body: Sam and his little sister June had been fighting over the big maple tree in the backyard all summer. Sam said it was his because he climbed it first. June said it was hers because she named it. They drew a chalk line across the trunk and argued about which side the best branch was on. Finally their grandfather, who was visiting, called them both to the porch. He went inside and came back with a folded paper from their father's desk. It was the deed to the house. He showed them that the yard, and the tree, belonged to their mom and dad. The kids were quiet for a moment, a little embarrassed. Then Grandpa smiled and said there was more. Even Mom and Dad did not really own it. Yahweh is the Most High, the Possessor of heaven and earth. The deed in the drawer only lasts a few years. His title lasts forever. That meant the tree was His, and they were just taking care of it for Him while they lived there. June asked if Yahweh minded who climbed it. Grandpa laughed and said He probably cared more about whether they were kind to each other in it. Sam looked at the chalk line on the trunk. Then he went and got a bucket of water and scrubbed it off. That afternoon they built a little bench under the maple together, and they planted flowers around its roots. Neither of them ever called it my tree again. They called it the Lord's tree, and they took very good care of it.

gh-el-elyon-possessor.title: The Contract He Would Not Sign
gh-el-elyon-possessor.body: Nathaniel Ortiz ran a small construction company, and he had prayed for two years for a big break. Then it came. A wealthy developer named Mr. Crane offered him the biggest contract of his life, enough to pay off every debt and hire six more men. There was only one condition, spoken softly over an expensive lunch. Nathaniel would build only for Crane from now on, look the other way at a few shortcuts, and never forget who had made him rich. Nathaniel drove home with the contract on the seat beside him. That night he could not sleep. He read about Abram, who had been offered the riches of a king, and had refused to take anything at all, so that no one could ever say a man had made him rich. Abram had lifted his hand to the Most High, the Possessor of heaven and earth. Nathaniel sat with that a long time. If Yahweh truly owned heaven and earth, then there was no ground outside His title. Not the company, not the trucks, not the debts, not Nathaniel himself. He was not a man waiting for a rich patron. He was a steward of what was already His. The next morning he called Mr. Crane and politely said no. His foreman thought he had lost his mind. The next year was lean. But one by one, families and churches came to him because they heard he could not be bought. The company grew slowly, honestly, and debt-free. When people asked how he had built it, Nathaniel always said the same thing. He had not built it. He was only taking care of it for the Owner.

gh-el-shaddai-almighty.title: One Lantern Length
gh-el-shaddai-almighty.body: Abby was eight the night her father took her out to check on the calves in the far pasture. There was no moon, and the path between the barn and the field was black as ink. Her father handed her the lantern. Abby held it up and frowned. It only lit a small circle around her feet, maybe ten steps ahead. She said she could not see the gate, or the field, or the calves. How was she supposed to walk when she could not see where she was going? Her father laughed softly. He said she did not need to see the gate. She only needed to see the next ten steps, and when she took them, the light would go with her and show her ten more. He was walking right beside her, and he knew the whole way. So Abby walked. Ten steps, and ten more, and ten more, until the gate came out of the dark exactly where her father said it would be. That fall Abby started a new school, and she was worried about everything. What if she got lost? What if she had no friends? What if the work was too hard? Her father reminded her of the lantern. Yahweh is Almighty, he said, and He knows the whole road. He usually shows us just enough for the next steps, and asks us to walk with Him in those. Abby thought about it. The next morning she did not ask to see the whole year. She only asked Yahweh for help with the first day. And then, when it came, the second.

gh-el-shaddai-almighty.title: The Plan He Demanded
gh-el-shaddai-almighty.body: When Douglas Fry's father began to forget things, Douglas felt Yahweh nudging him to move the old man into his own home. Douglas did not want to. He had a career, a schedule, and a hundred questions. How long would it last? What would it cost? Would his marriage survive it? So he told the Lord he would obey as soon as he could see the whole plan. Until then he would wait. He waited a year. His father fell twice living alone. Douglas kept asking for the whole picture, and the whole picture did not come. Only the same quiet nudge, the same next step. One night his pastor read a passage about how Yahweh had shown Himself to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as El Shaddai, the Almighty, and had not yet made Himself known to them by His covenant name. They walked with Him faithfully anyway, with the part they had been given. Douglas sat in the pew and felt ashamed. He had been calling his delay wisdom. It was really a demand for proof. The Lord was not hiding the plan from him. He was pacing it, and the next step had been plain for a year. Douglas moved his father in that spring. It was harder than he had imagined, and it was also more beautiful. He learned patience, and to laugh at the same story told five times. His teenage son learned to shave his grandfather. Douglas never did get the whole plan in advance. But by the end, looking back, he could see that each step had been given right when he needed it.

gh-i-am-that-i-am.title: What Would His Name Tag Say
gh-i-am-that-i-am.body: At the Willow Creek church picnic, everyone got a sticker name tag that said I AM at the top, with a blank line underneath. People wrote things like I am Linda, I am the Thompsons' neighbor, I am the pie lady. Seven-year-old Rosie wrote I am Rosie, I am the fastest girl in second grade. Then she sat on the picnic blanket next to her grandmother and asked a question that had been bothering her. What would Yahweh write on His name tag? Her grandmother set down her lemonade. That, she said, is a very good question, and Moses asked almost the same one. He wanted to know what name to tell the people. And the answer Yahweh gave was just I AM. Rosie wrinkled her nose. I am what? Nothing after it, said her grandmother. Every one of our tags needs something after the line, because we are only what we are because of other things. Rosie is fast because she has strong legs, and legs can get hurt. The pie lady is the pie lady because she has an oven. But Yahweh does not need anything after the line. He does not come from anything. He just is, and nothing can ever be taken away from Him. Rosie thought about that while she watched the sack race. Then she took off her name tag and crossed out the fastest girl in second grade. Underneath, in careful letters, she wrote I am His. Her grandmother asked why. Rosie said because that one could not get hurt.

gh-i-am-that-i-am.title: Everything That Could Be Taken
gh-i-am-that-i-am.body: Corinne Abbott had built her life on good, solid things. A husband of forty years. A house by the river that her father had built. A savings account, a garden, a church where she had sat in the same pew since she was a girl. Then, in a single year, they began to go. Her husband died in the spring. In the summer, floodwaters filled the house to the windowsills, and the insurance paid only part of the loss. In the fall her church merged with another across town, and her old pew was carried off and sold. Corinne sat in a borrowed apartment surrounded by boxes and felt as though the floor of the world had dropped away. Every good thing she had leaned on had turned out to be something that could be taken. One night she opened her Bible to the place where Moses stood before the burning bush and asked Yahweh His name. She had read it many times. That night she read it as if for the first time. The answer was not a place, or a river, or a thing that could flood. It was only I AM. He did not come from anything. He did not depend on anything. There was nothing He leaned on that could ever be swept away. Corinne set the book down and wept, and then, strangely, she felt the floor come back under her feet. Everything else had been given and could be taken. He simply was. In the years that followed, she rebuilt slowly. But she never again rested her weight on the boxes. She rested it on Him.

gh-babel-make-us-a-name.title: The Tower With Leo's Name on It
gh-babel-make-us-a-name.body: In Mrs. Grant's third-grade class, the students had one hour to build the tallest tower they could out of wooden blocks. Leo was determined to win. He built fast and high, and when his tower reached past his shoulders, he grabbed a marker and a strip of paper and wrote LEO in giant letters and taped it to the very top. He wanted everyone in the school to know whose tower it was. Then he kept going. Higher. Wobblier. He would not let anyone help, because then it would not be his. When it fell, it fell all at once, blocks bouncing across the floor and under the desks. The paper with his name on it floated down and landed in the trash can. Leo was furious, and then he was embarrassed, and then he cried. That evening he told his grandmother about it. She listened and then asked him if he knew where his name came from. He did not. She told him his mother had picked it while she was still carrying him, and his father had said it out loud for the first time in the hospital, holding him. Nobody had to build it, she said. It was given to you, with love, before you ever did a single thing. You never have to tape it to the top of anything to make it real. Leo thought about that for a long while. The next week the class built towers again, in teams. Leo's team built a short, wide, sturdy one, and nobody wrote their name on it. It was the only tower still standing at the end.

gh-babel-make-us-a-name.title: The Letters on the Roof
gh-babel-make-us-a-name.body: Victor Strand had his name put on top of his building in steel letters six feet tall. He had grown up poor and ignored, and he had promised himself that one day everyone in the city would know who he was. So he climbed. He worked eighteen hours a day. He outmaneuvered partners, crushed rivals, and paid people to write flattering things about him. Every new achievement had to be guarded, because someone was always trying to tear it down. He could never rest. A name you built yourself, he discovered, had to be defended forever. When his business partner sued him and the newspapers turned on him, Victor sat alone in his top-floor office under his own giant name and realized he had no one to call. His grown son had stopped speaking to him years before. Late that night he found himself in a small chapel near the office, where an old minister was turning off the lights. Victor told him everything. The minister did not flatter him or condemn him. He told Victor that he had spent his life trying to climb up and give himself a name. But Yahweh gives names. He had changed Abram's name to Abraham as a gift. And through Jesus He gives a new name, His child, to anyone who will stop climbing and receive it. Victor knelt on the chapel floor and stopped climbing. A month later he had the steel letters taken down. He sold the building and used the money to repay those he had wronged. Then he drove to his son's house and knocked. For the first time in his life, Victor Strand had nothing to defend.

gh-nations-divided-portion.title: Mr. Bell's Own Plot
gh-nations-divided-portion.body: Nora was nine and had been living with her new family for only three months when they signed up for a plot at the community garden. The garden belonged to old Mr. Bell, who had drawn it all out himself. Every family got a square with string and stakes around it, so nobody had to argue about where their beans ended and the neighbors' began. Mr. Bell had set every boundary carefully, and he walked the rows each morning to make sure everyone had what they needed. But there was one plot in the middle of the garden that was not rented to anybody. It had roses and an apple tree and a little wooden bench. Nora asked him whose it was. Mr. Bell smiled. That one is mine, he said. I gave all the others out. That one I keep, and I tend it myself. Nora watched him kneel in the dirt and pull weeds from around the roses, slow and careful, as if there was nothing in the world he would rather do. On the walk home Nora was quiet. Then she asked her new mother whether she was like the rented plots or like Mr. Bell's. Her mother stopped on the sidewalk and knelt down so they were eye to eye. She said Yahweh had set the borders of every nation in the world, and none of them were loose or forgotten. But He kept His own people for Himself, like Mr. Bell's plot, and He tends them with His own hands. You are His, she said. And you are ours. Not rented. Kept. Nora held her hand the rest of the way home.

gh-nations-divided-portion.title: Who He Answered To
gh-nations-divided-portion.body: For most of his life Terrence Webb had lived like a man nobody owned. He drifted from job to job and church to church. He changed his opinions to fit whoever was paying him or whoever he wanted to impress. He did not think of it as a weakness. He thought of it as freedom. Then, at forty-five, he came to faith in Jesus in a small church that met in a school gym, and the pastor said something one Sunday that Terrence could not shake. The pastor taught that the Most High had set the boundaries of every nation on earth, so that nothing anywhere was loose or forgotten, and that He had kept His own people as His portion, handed off to no one. Terrence realized he had never belonged to anyone. And now he did. A few weeks later his supervisor at the warehouse told him to sign off on a shipment report he knew was false. The old Terrence would have signed it without a second thought. He had always answered to whoever stood in front of him. But he was not unclaimed anymore. He told the supervisor, quietly, that he could not sign it. He was written up for it. He went home shaken and prayed in his truck in the driveway, and to his surprise he was not afraid. Two months later the supervisor was let go, and the company manager called Terrence into the office and asked him to run the floor. Terrence knew exactly who he worked for now. It was not the manager.

gh-borrowed-crown.title: The Whistle Felix Bought
gh-borrowed-crown.body: Felix spent his entire birthday money on a black-and-white striped shirt and a shiny silver whistle. The next day at recess he wore them both out to the kickball field and announced that he was the referee now. At first it worked. Kids stopped when he blew the whistle. They waited for his calls. Felix loved it. He made calls that helped his friends and hurt kids he did not like. He blew the whistle just to watch everyone freeze. Then one afternoon there was a real argument. A girl named Tess kicked the ball, and nobody could agree whether it was fair or foul. Felix blew his whistle and called it foul. And for the first time, nobody listened. Tess said he was not really the referee. He had just bought a shirt. A boy named Marcus agreed. Felix blew the whistle harder, but the argument only grew louder, until Mr. Ruiz, the playground teacher, walked over. Every kid on the field turned to him at once. Nobody had to tell them to. They knew Mr. Ruiz. He had been fair to all of them all year, and the principal had given him the job. He watched the replay in his head, called it fair, and the game went on. Felix stood at the edge of the field holding his whistle, red in the face. Later Mr. Ruiz sat with him on the bench. He told Felix that a shirt can make you look like a referee, but only being trusted and being given the job makes you one. Felix gave the whistle to his little brother. He kept the shirt for pajamas.

gh-borrowed-crown.title: The Wall of Plaques
gh-borrowed-crown.body: When Elsie Grimes's husband died, a man named Mr. Sterling began calling on her. He was a financial adviser, he said, and he invited her to his office downtown. It was grand. There were marble floors, leather chairs, and an entire wall covered in gold plaques and framed certificates. There were photos of him shaking hands with important-looking people. Elsie, who had never handled money before, felt small and grateful. He offered to manage her life savings. She nearly signed that afternoon. That Sunday she told her grandson Peter about it. Peter was quiet a moment and then asked a simple question. Who gave him all those plaques? Elsie did not know. So Peter looked. It took him two evenings. Most of the certificates came from organizations that did not exist, and the rest could be bought by anyone for a fee. The photos had been taken at public events. Mr. Sterling had dressed himself in the look of a trustworthy man without ever being given the trust. Elsie did not sign. A year later Mr. Sterling's office closed, and many people lost a great deal. Elsie thought often about that wall of plaques and about the gods of Egypt, which had covered the walls of a whole kingdom and had not protected anyone when Yahweh brought judgment. Impressive things could still be empty things. She took her savings instead to Walt Henley, a plain man at her church who had quietly helped widows for thirty years and had nothing on his walls at all. And Elsie began asking the same question of herself. Not how she looked, but who she belonged to.

gh-knowledge-and-sin.title: The Seedlings by the Fence
gh-knowledge-and-sin.body: Mateo and his friends played ball every afternoon in the empty lot behind Mrs. Kowalski's house. One Saturday, chasing a long throw, Mateo slid right through a patch of tiny green sprouts along the fence and flattened half of them. He had no idea they were there. Mrs. Kowalski came out on her porch with her hand over her heart. She had planted those tomato seedlings that week for her grandchildren. Mateo's face went hot. He blurted out that he did not know, so it was not his fault. That evening he told his father the whole story, still saying it was not fair to blame him. His father listened and nodded. He said Mateo was right that not knowing mattered. If he had stomped on them on purpose, that would have been far worse. But the seedlings were still crushed, and Mateo was still the one who crushed them. Not knowing made it lighter. It did not make it nothing. So what do you do now that you know? Mateo thought about it. The next morning he knocked on Mrs. Kowalski's door, said he was sorry, and offered to help her replant. She handed him a trowel. He spent the whole afternoon on his knees in the dirt beside her, and she taught him how deep to set each one, and which plants liked sun. By the end of the summer Mateo knew every row in her garden by name. When a new boy chased a ball toward the fence one day, Mateo shouted a warning before he got close. Knowing, he had discovered, was not a trap. It was a job.

gh-knowledge-and-sin.title: What the Ledger Showed
gh-knowledge-and-sin.body: Harriet Osei owned a small clothing shop that she was proud of. Her prices were fair, her customers loved her, and she gave generously at church. Then a reporter's question at a town meeting sent her digging through her supplier's records, and what she found made her sick. The company that sewed her best-selling shirts was paying its workers far too little and keeping them at the machines for impossibly long hours. For eight years she had been selling their labor without knowing it. Her first thought was a relief that shamed her: she had not known, so it was not her sin. Her second thought came that night and crushed her: she was no better than the company itself, and eight years of profit were stained beyond repair. She could not sleep. She went to her pastor, an old man named Brother James, and told him both thoughts. He shook his head gently at each one. Not knowing, he said, did not mean the wrong never happened. It had happened, and she had taken part in it. But not knowing did make the weight lighter than if she had done it on purpose, and Yahweh is just, and He measures fairly. The real question now was what she would do with what she knew. Much was being required because much had been given. Harriet went home and wrote three letters. She ended the contract. She found a supplier that paid fairly, even though it cost her more. And she sent part of her profit from the past eight years to a group that helped those very workers. Then, for the first time in weeks, she slept.

gh-remedy-that-arrives-on-a-calendar.title: The Corner of the Orchard
gh-remedy-that-arrives-on-a-calendar.body: Mr. Harmon's apple orchard sat at the edge of town, and every autumn he did something the other orchard owners called foolish. He left the whole last row of trees along the road unpicked. No sign. No sign-up sheet. No one had to ask. Anyone who needed apples could simply come and take them. Widows came with baskets. A family who had just moved into the shelter came with grocery bags. Kids on bikes stopped on the way home from school. Mr. Harmon also ran the general store, and he had another strange habit. On the first day of every seventh year, he took out his ledger and crossed off every small debt in it. Nobody had to come in and beg. Nobody had to prove they were struggling. It simply happened on the calendar, like Christmas. One fall his granddaughter Lucy, who was ten, asked him why he did not just help people when they asked. Mr. Harmon set down his ladder and thought about it. He said the people who need help most are often the ones who will never ask. Some are too proud, some are too tired, and some do not even know they can. If help only comes to the ones who complain loudest, then the quietest people never get any. So Yahweh taught His people to put the help on a schedule, built right into the field and the calendar, where nobody has to fight for it. Lucy looked down the road at old Mrs. Fields, who had come every year since her husband died and never said a word. She was filling her basket, smiling.

gh-remedy-that-arrives-on-a-calendar.title: The Woman Who Never Complained
gh-remedy-that-arrives-on-a-calendar.body: Simon Hart owned a dozen small rental houses, and he thought of himself as a fair landlord. When tenants had trouble, he told them, they only needed to come and talk to him, and he would work something out. Some did. They called, explained, pushed back, and he usually lowered their late fees. He felt good about it. Then one winter he was going through old files and found the account of Dorothy Lane, a widow who had rented from him for eleven years. She had never once called to complain. And because she had never asked, she had paid every late fee, every charge for repairs that should have been his, every increase, in full, for over a decade, some months skipping her own medicine to do it. Simon sat at his desk for a long time with her file in his hands. His mercy only reached the people strong enough to fight for it. The weakest person he rented to had gotten none at all. That week he read in the Word how Yahweh had commanded a release every seven years, built right into the calendar, so that the poorest did not have to plead their case to be set free. Simon did not wait to be asked. He went to Dorothy's house himself, explained what he had found, and returned every fee she had overpaid. She wept at her kitchen table. Then he changed his whole system. Every January, now, every account is reviewed whether anyone complains or not. Fees are released on a schedule. Simon never again waited for the quiet ones to come knocking. He had learned to go to them first.

gh-one-mediator.title: Marcus and the List of Tricks
gh-one-mediator.body: Marcus was nine when he decided he wanted to talk to Yahweh, really talk, and he was sure there must be a trick to it. So he made a list. His friend Tyler said you had to close your eyes so tight you saw sparks. A girl on the bus said you had to say it three times or it did not count. His cousin said you needed a candle and a quiet room and a special way of breathing. Marcus tried all of it one Saturday afternoon, sparks and candle and breathing, and when nothing happened he came into the kitchen looking like a boy whose kite had snapped its string. His grandmother was snapping beans at the table. She listened to the whole list, nodding. Then she pointed out the window at her tomato vine, heavy and green, and at one branch the wind had broken off that morning, lying limp in the dirt. "That branch did not need a trick," she said. "It needed to stay on the vine. There is one door to the Father, baby, and His name is Jesus, and the door is already open. You do not have to climb anything. You just come through Him." Marcus looked at the list in his hand. Then he folded it up, sat down across from her, bowed his head over the beans, and said, "Jesus, it is me, Marcus." He did not see sparks. He did not need to. He was talking, and he knew he was heard, and that afternoon he talked a long time.

gh-one-mediator.title: The Woman Who Paid to Be Heard
gh-one-mediator.body: After her husband died, Ruth could not feel anything when she prayed, and she took the silence as a locked door. So she went looking for a key. She paid for a weekend retreat that promised to raise her awareness to a higher level. She bought recordings that taught her to quiet her mind in seven stages. A smiling guide told her she had spirit guides waiting, if only she would tune herself finely enough to reach them. Every method added one more step between her and the One she wanted, and every step she failed made her more certain that she was not good enough to be heard. Her savings shrank. Her hope shrank faster. One evening her old friend Bernice found her crying over a workbook full of exercises and sat down beside her. Bernice did not argue with the workbook. She simply asked, "Ruth, who did you used to pray to, before all this?" Ruth whispered, "Jesus." "Then He is still the way in," Bernice said. "There is one go-between, and He already did all the going. You do not have to qualify. You do not have to tune anything. You only have to come to the Father through Him." That night Ruth closed the workbook and prayed the way she had as a girl, plainly, in the name of Jesus. She still felt nothing. But for the first time in a year she did not treat the nothing as an answer. She had been heard, because He had promised to hear, and she slept.

gh-spirit-bears-witness-with.title: Caleb's Compass
gh-spirit-bears-witness-with.body: Caleb was sixteen and had a decision to make about which summer job to take, and someone at a youth retreat had told him the answer was already inside him. "Just ask your spirit," the boy had said. "Get really quiet and it will tell you." So Caleb sat on his bed for an hour with his eyes shut, waiting for a briefing. He heard the refrigerator hum. He heard his sister practicing piano. He heard his own worries, very loudly, arguing in circles. Nothing else. Frustrated, he went out to the garage, where his uncle Ray was sorting fishing tackle, and told him the whole thing. Ray dug in a tackle box and pulled out an old brass compass. "Does this make north?" he asked. Caleb frowned. "No. It just points to it." "Right," Ray said. "Your spirit is real, and it is a good instrument. But it is a witness, not the one who knows. If you want to know what Yahweh wants, you go to His Spirit and to His Word, and you ask Him. Then your spirit will tell you it agrees." That night Caleb opened the Word and read slowly, then prayed and asked the Holy Spirit to lead him. He did not get a voice in the dark. But as he read about serving, something in him settled, quiet and sure, toward the job at the camp for younger kids. It was not his own idea coming back to him. It was agreement. Two witnesses, and his was the second one.

gh-spirit-bears-witness-with.title: The Bad Week
gh-spirit-bears-witness-with.body: Adele had been a believer for twenty years, and in one gray February week she became certain she was not one at all. Nothing had happened. She had not done anything terrible. She simply woke one morning heavy, and the heaviness stayed, and inside the heaviness a voice in her own head kept saying that if she were really His child she would feel it, and she did not feel it, so she must not be. By Thursday she had stopped answering her phone. Her friend Joanne came by anyway with a pot of soup and found her at the kitchen table, unwashed coffee cups all around her. Adele told her everything in a flat voice. Joanne listened, then set the soup down and took her hand. "Adele, you are treating your own feelings like the only witness in the courtroom," she said gently. "They are a witness. They are not the only one. The Holy Spirit testifies too, and He does not have bad weeks." Adele looked at her for a long time. "So my standing does not depend on how I feel today?" "It never did," Joanne said. "Your heart says amen when it can. On the days it cannot, His witness still stands." Something loosened. The heaviness did not lift that afternoon, and Joanne made her call her doctor too, which she did. But the low mood stopped being evidence. Adele was tired, and she was sad, and she was still the Father's daughter, and on the bad days that was enough to stand on.

gh-whole-spirit-soul-body.title: Walter Skips Dinner
gh-whole-spirit-soul-body.body: Walter came home from a Saturday seminar fired up and announced to his wife that he was going to make his spirit rule his body. No more giving in to tiredness. No more being bossed around by hunger. He would sleep four hours a night and skip supper, and pray instead, and become a giant of faith. His wife, Marjorie, raised one eyebrow and said nothing. The first night went well. The second night he fell asleep during his own prayer and woke with his face on the Bible. By Wednesday he was so hungry and foggy that he locked his keys in the truck, put the milk in the cupboard, and called his grandson by the dog's name. On Thursday Marjorie set a bowl of chicken soup in front of him and sat down across the table. "Walter," she said, "Yahweh made your body. He did not make it to be beaten into line. He keeps all of you, the inside and the outside both." Walter stared at the soup. Then he opened his Bible to where he had fallen asleep on it, and read, and realized it never once told him to rank his parts and wage war on the bottom one. It told him he was kept, whole. He ate the soup. He went to bed at nine. In the morning he prayed for an hour with a clear head and a full stomach, and it was the best hour of prayer he had had all week. Marjorie only smiled into her coffee.

gh-whole-spirit-soul-body.title: The Long Illness
gh-whole-spirit-soul-body.body: For three years Grace had been sick, and for most of those three years she believed the sickness was her fault. Someone at a prayer meeting had told her that if her spirit were strong enough, her body would have to obey, and the words had lodged in her like a splinter. So every morning she lay in bed and searched herself. Was there a hidden sin? A weak spot in her faith? A part of her soul that was out of order? She sorted and resorted her own heart like a drawer of tangled thread, and the searching never ended, because there was always another knot. One afternoon a deacon named Mr. Oduya came to visit, as he did every Tuesday. He found her exhausted, not from the illness but from the searching. When she told him why, he was quiet for a while. Then he said, "Grace, you were not given the job of dividing yourself up. That is the Word's work, not yours. And Yahweh keeps the whole of you. Your spirit, your soul, and this tired body too. Being sick is not a verdict on your faith." He opened his Bible and read to her, and she listened, and for once she let the reading do what her own digging never could. Her body stayed weak for a long while yet. But the war inside her ended that day. She took her medicine without shame, rested without guilt, and prayed without inspecting herself first. She was kept, all three parts of her, and she knew it.

gh-inside-love.title: Ben Moves In
gh-inside-love.body: Ben was the new boy in fifth grade, and he wore his hood up even indoors, the way some people wear armor. His friend Eli's family invited him to dinner once a month, and once a month Ben came, ate fast, said very little, and left the minute his plate was clean. He liked it there. He just did not trust it. Love that you visit is easy to stop believing in once you are back out in the cold. Then in June his mother had to work out of state for the summer, and Eli's parents asked if Ben would like to stay with them. Ben shrugged, which meant yes. The first week he kept his hood up at the table. The second week Eli's little sister asked him to read her a bedtime story, and he did, hood and all. By the third week he was laughing at Eli's dad's terrible jokes, and by the fourth he had forgotten he even owned the hood. Nothing magic had happened. He had simply stopped visiting the warm house and started living in it, waking up in it, eating breakfast in it, being forgiven in it when he broke a glass. At the end of summer Eli's mother hugged him goodbye and said, "You know you live here now, right? Even when you are home. That is how the Father loves you too, Ben. You can visit it, or you can live in it." Ben nodded. He did know. And the strange thing was, when he got back to his own apartment, it did not feel so cold anymore. He had brought the warmth with him, because now he knew where he lived.

gh-inside-love.title: Frank Changes His Address
gh-inside-love.body: Frank had been cheated twice in business, once by a partner and once by a bank, and he had come out of it with a heart like a frozen pond. He was polite. He paid his bills. He went to church at Easter and Christmas, sat in the back, and left before the last song. Love, to him, was a building you stopped by on holidays, nothing more. One November his neighbor Mrs. Castillo asked if he would help unload a truck at the church food pantry, because her son had hurt his back. Frank said yes only because he could not think of a polite no. He carried boxes for two hours, and a little boy in line thanked him by name, and something in Frank cracked very slightly. He came back the next week. Then the week after. He started reading the Word in the mornings, not to study but to believe it, that Yahweh actually loved him, Frank, the cold man in the back pew. He started praying for the partner who had cheated him. He started noticing faces at the pantry, and then names, and then stories. A year later Mrs. Castillo watched him kneel down to tie a child's shoe and could hardly believe it was the same man. "What happened to you?" she asked. Frank thought about it. "I used to visit," he said. "Now I live there." He had moved into love the way a man moves into a house, and found that the One who is Love had moved into him.

gh-die-daily.title: Grandpa Amos Lays It Down
gh-die-daily.body: Every morning before breakfast, Grandpa Amos stood on the back porch with his coffee for exactly five minutes, and his grandchildren had always assumed he was looking at the birds. One summer Lily, who was eleven, finally asked him. "I am laying things down," he said. "What things?" He counted on his fingers. "My right to be first in line. My right to be offended when somebody cuts me off at the feed store. My idea of how today should go. I put the old Amos down every morning, before he gets a chance to run the day." Lily thought that sounded strange until she watched it work. That afternoon a man took the parking space Grandpa had been waiting for, and Grandpa just waved and found another. At supper Grandma changed the plans for Saturday, and Grandpa said, "Sounds good to me," and meant it. When the pickup broke down on the highway, he sat on the tailgate humming while they waited for the tow. "Doesn't anything bother you?" Lily asked. He laughed. "Plenty tries. But it is hard to offend a man who already gave up his rights at seven this morning." The next day Lily joined him on the porch with her orange juice. She did not know exactly what she was laying down. Her temper, maybe, and wanting to be right about everything with her brother. But she stood there five minutes, and that afternoon when her brother teased her, she let it go, and she felt lighter than she could explain.

gh-die-daily.title: Miss Hattie Was Packed
gh-die-daily.body: Miss Hattie lived to ninety-one, and when the doctor told her family the end was near, her granddaughter Simone drove all night expecting to find chaos. She found order instead. The will was signed and in the top drawer. The quilts had little tags pinned to them, one for each grandchild. Every letter Miss Hattie owed had been written. There was not one old grudge left unsettled in the whole family; she had made her peace with her sister forty years ago and with the neighbor over the fence line twenty years ago. Simone sat by the bed and held her thin hand. "Grandma, how are you not afraid?" Miss Hattie smiled. "Baby, I have been dying every morning for sixty years. I put myself down before breakfast. My pride, my wants, my right to have things my way. I took up His way instead, every single day. So there is nothing left in me that is scared to let go. I already let go. This is just the last time." Simone cried, and Miss Hattie let her, patting her hand. "This world was never Home," she said softly. "I have been living packed. When He calls, I am ready to walk out the door." She went to be with Jesus three days later, early in the morning, peaceful as a sunrise. And Simone, driving home after the funeral, pulled over at a rest stop just after dawn, stood beside her car, and began to lay things down.

gh-kenosis.title: The Captain Who Played Defense
gh-kenosis.body: Nia was the best scorer on her soccer team, and everyone assumed that in her final season she would be captain and play up front, where the glory was. Then the coach pulled her aside. The team was losing because nobody could hold the back line, and he asked if she would move to defense. Defense meant no goals. No name in the paper. No cheers. Just hard, plain work that nobody noticed unless it went wrong. Nia went home and sulked through dinner. Her father, who had been listening, asked her a question. "Who stepped down from the highest place there is?" She knew the answer. Jesus had come off the Throne of Glory, become a man, and obeyed the Father all the way to the cross. And because He went down, the Father lifted Him up. "So I am supposed to play defense," she said. "I think you are supposed to obey," her father said. "Down is the way up." The next week Nia played defense. She hated it at first. Then she learned it. By mid-season the team had stopped losing, and the younger girls, watching her dive for every ball without complaint, started playing harder too. At the end-of-season dinner the coach stood up to name the captain for the all-star game. He did not pick the top scorer. He said, "I am picking the girl who stepped down when we asked her to." And he called Nia's name, and the whole room stood up.

gh-kenosis.title: The Pastor Who Went Small
gh-kenosis.body: Pastor Simmons led a church of three thousand in the city, with a choir and a radio program and his name on a sign out front. He was good at it, and he loved it, and one winter, in prayer, he became certain that Yahweh was asking him to leave it. Out in the farm country, an hour north, a little white church had eleven members left and no pastor at all. Nobody understood. His board pleaded with him. Some friends called it foolish. His own pride called it worse things in the night. But he kept thinking about the Son, who had all the Glory there is and set it aside, who became a servant and obeyed the Father all the way to the cross. If the King had stepped down, the servant could.
