I'm going to sit down with each of you and go over your week." Ivy nodded happily. "I've got all of Sam's notes ready." "That's kind of you," her father said, "but I won't need them. Tomorrow I'm only going to ask you about your chart." Ivy blinked. She went to look at it. Her own boxes were half empty. While she had been inspecting Sam's room, her own had turned into a jungle. While she had been counting his socks, her goldfish had gone two days without food. That night she put down the clipboard and got to work. She fed the fish, made her bed, sorted her laundry, and even swept the porch, which was not on the chart at all. On Saturday her father went over her week with her, and she was glad to show him. At church the next morning the pastor said that one day every one of us will stand before Jesus and give an account, not of our neighbor's life, but of our own. Ivy looked over at Sam and grinned. Then she quietly slipped her old clipboard into the recycling bin on the way out.

gh-judgment-seat-of-christ.title: Marjorie's Notebook
gh-judgment-seat-of-christ.body: Marjorie Fenn had kept the books at Cedar Hill Church for twenty years, and she kept another book too, a small spiral notebook in her purse. In it she wrote what she noticed about other people: who left early, who gave less than they could afford, who sang off key on purpose, which deacon's son had been seen at the lake on a Sunday. She never showed it to anyone. She only read it to herself on hard nights, and it made her feel that someone, at least, was keeping things straight. One autumn the pastor preached on the judgment seat of Christ. He said that every believer will one day stand before Jesus Himself and give an account of what was done in this life, the good and the bad, and that the Son will review His own family's stewardship. He said each of us will answer for one life only, our own. Marjorie went home and took out the notebook. For the first time she asked herself what account she would give. She thought of her neighbor, Mrs. Doyle, widowed two years and living alone across the street, to whom Marjorie had not carried so much as a casserole. She thought of her sister, whose calls she let ring. She thought of the hours she had spent watching others and the hours she had spent on her own heart, and the second number was very small. That night Marjorie tore the pages out of the notebook one by one and burned them in the fireplace. Then she wrote on the first clean page: Things I will do this week. The first line said: Mrs. Doyle, soup, Tuesday. She found, to her surprise, that she slept better than she had in years.

gh-vacate-the-seat.title: Mrs. Pruitt's Porch
gh-vacate-the-seat.body: From her front porch, Mrs. Pruitt could see the whole of Hawthorne Lane, and she had an opinion about every yard on it. The Bakers let their dog bark. The Nguyens painted their door too bright. But the house she judged most was the one right across the street, where a man named Mr. Carey lived. His grass was knee high. His gutters sagged. His mailbox leaned like a tired old man. "Lazy," Mrs. Pruitt said to anyone who would listen. "Plain lazy. Some people just don't care." She said it at the grocery store and at the beauty shop and once, loudly, at the church potluck. One evening in July a storm knocked out the power on the whole street. Mrs. Pruitt saw a candle flickering in Mr. Carey's window and, out of habit, went over to see what he was up to. She found him in the back room beside a hospital bed, spooning water to his wife, who had been sick for two years. He had been caring for her day and night, alone, too tired to mow and too proud to ask for help. Mrs. Pruitt stood in the doorway a long time. She had passed a verdict on a man without knowing a single thing that was hidden inside his house. On the walk home she prayed, and told Jesus that she was stepping down from a seat that had never been hers. That case was His, and always had been. The next Saturday Mrs. Pruitt's grandsons mowed the Careys' lawn. On Monday she brought supper. And from her porch, after that, she found she mostly watched the sunset instead.

gh-vacate-the-seat.title: The Son Martin Gave Up On
gh-vacate-the-seat.body: When Martin Shaw's son Nathan left home at nineteen, he left angry, and he took his father's truck and two thousand dollars from the drawer. In the years that followed, the reports that drifted back were all bad: a lost job, a night in a county cell, a string of rented rooms. Martin decided the matter was closed. At church, when people asked, he said it flatly: "He's gone. He made his choice. He'll never amount to anything." He said it so often that he began to believe he had the right to say it. But carrying that verdict cost him. Martin grew bitter. He could not hear the boy's name without his jaw tightening. He lay awake rehearsing the case, every wrong his son had done, like a lawyer who could never quite finish his closing argument. One Sunday an old friend, Gerald, sat with him on the church steps. "Martin," he said quietly, "you've been sitting in a chair that belongs to Someone else. Nathan isn't your servant to sentence. He belongs to the Lord. And the Lord is able to make him stand." Martin wanted to argue. Instead he went home and, for the first time in six years, he prayed for his son instead of about him. He told Jesus he was handing the case over, the whole file, and getting out of the judge's seat. The bitterness did not leave all at once, but it began to leave. Four years later there was a knock at Martin's door. Nathan stood on the step, thinner and older, holding a small Bible and a check for two thousand dollars. "I met Jesus, Dad," he said. Martin did not say a word. He just opened his arms.

gh-saints-judge-with-him.title: The Fence Between Two Deacons
gh-saints-judge-with-him.body: Deacon Abbott and Deacon Reyes had farmed side by side for twenty years, and in all that time they had never once argued, until the spring a surveyor found that the old fence between their pastures stood eleven feet onto the Reyes land. Abbott's barn was inside those eleven feet. By June both men had called lawyers. By July the whole church was choosing sides, and the Sunday handshakes had gone stiff. Then Pastor Linden invited both men to his kitchen table on a Tuesday night. He did not take a side. He set out coffee and a plate of his wife's biscuits and said, "Brothers, before we hand this to a courtroom in town, let's see whether the family can settle a family matter. One day the people of Yahweh are going to help judge far bigger things than a fence line. Seems to me we ought to practice on the small ones." The two men sat stiffly for an hour. Then Reyes admitted he did not want the barn at all; he only wanted his cows to reach the creek. Abbott admitted he had been afraid of losing the barn his father built. By ten o'clock they had drawn a new line on a napkin: the barn stayed where it was, and a gate opened to the water for both herds. They shook hands over the biscuits. The lawyers were dismissed the next morning. That fall the two men built the new gate together on a Saturday, with half the church bringing lunch. Pastor Linden kept the napkin. He said it was the best ruling he had ever seen handed down, and he had not written a word of it.

gh-saints-judge-with-him.title: Isaac and the Folding Chairs
gh-saints-judge-with-him.body: Isaac Mendel was seventeen and sharper than most of the adults at Grace Fellowship. He could read people. He could see a problem coming a mile off. And he knew it. When the youth pastor moved away, Isaac assumed the job would naturally fall to him, and when the elders asked him instead to set up the folding chairs every Sunday and help settle squabbles among the fourth graders, he took it as an insult. For a while he made it obvious. He corrected the new youth leader in front of the kids, overruling decisions, gathering his own little following. He was right about many things, and that only made it worse. One evening the old pastor, Brother Amos, found him stacking chairs with a sour face. Amos sat down on one of them. "Isaac," he said, "Yahweh has a bench prepared for His people, seats where they will judge with Him, things bigger than you can imagine. But those seats are given, not grabbed. The training is right here. The man who can hold a real gift and not reach for the gavel early is the man who can be trusted with it later." Isaac said nothing. But the next Sunday he set out the chairs carefully, in straight rows, and when two fourth graders came to blows over a snack, he knelt between them and helped them make peace instead of making a ruling. He did that for six years. When the elders finally asked him to lead, he almost said no. Decades later, an old man himself, Isaac still set out a few chairs before every service. When people asked why, he smiled and said he was in training.

gh-testing-not-temptation.title: Rosa's First Hard Week
gh-testing-not-temptation.body: Rosa was sixteen when she got her first summer job, at a busy diner by the highway, and on her very first Saturday the other server called in sick. By ten in the morning Rosa was running eleven tables alone. She spilled coffee on a trucker, forgot a little boy's pancakes, and cried for exactly two minutes in the walk-in freezer. Standing there among the frozen peas, she prayed, half angry: "Why would You put me here?" Then she wiped her face and went back out. Something happened that afternoon that Rosa did not expect. She started to find a rhythm. She learned to carry three plates on one arm. She learned to smile at the grumpy man in booth four until he smiled back. At closing time the owner, Mrs. Haddad, counted the receipts twice and whistled. That night Rosa told her grandmother all about it. Her grandmother listened, nodding. "Yahweh didn't put you there so you'd fail, mija," she said. "He already knew how today would go. He let it come so you could see what He put in you. And notice, He sent you a way through it, every time it got to be too much: the cook who helped you, the customer who was patient, that two minutes in the freezer to catch your breath." Rosa thought about it. It was true. Every time she had thought she would break, there had been a door. The next week Mrs. Haddad asked her to train the new girl. Rosa said yes, and when the new girl panicked on her first rush, Rosa took her by the elbow and said, "You can do more than you think. I'll show you the way through."

gh-testing-not-temptation.title: The Bookkeeper's Hard Month
gh-testing-not-temptation.body: Ray Dalton kept the books for a lumber yard, and in all his years there he had never been short a penny. Then came the winter his car died, his daughter needed braces, and the furnace went out in the same month. Ray sat at his desk late one night looking at the cash box, which held more than enough to cover all of it. No one would check until spring. He could put it back by then. He told himself it would only be borrowing. He told himself something else too, in a bitter whisper: that Yahweh had put him in this spot, that it was a test he had been set up to fail. But even as he said it, Ray knew it was not true. Nobody had put that cash box in front of him to make him a thief. The pull was coming from inside him, from his own fear and wanting. Yahweh does not lure a man toward evil. Ray took his hand off the box and sat back, shaking. And then, sitting there, he remembered something he had forgotten in his panic. His church had a benevolence fund for exactly this kind of winter. And his boss, old Mr. Whitlow, had told him once that the yard would always advance an honest man his pay. The way out had been there the whole time, built before the trouble ever came. He had only been looking at the box. The next morning Ray asked Mr. Whitlow for an advance and called the church. Both said yes. That spring, when the books were checked, they balanced to the penny, and Ray slept like a child.

gh-all-things-work-together.title: The Late Planting
gh-all-things-work-together.body: Every farmer in the valley planted corn in the second week of April, and Gus Henley had planned to do the same, until his tractor's transmission gave out on the first morning of planting. The part had to come from three states away. Gus stood in the barn with grease up to his elbows and said a word his wife made him apologize for. Then he sat on an overturned bucket and prayed. He told Yahweh he did not understand, and that he was choosing to trust Him anyway. His neighbors finished planting and went to church smiling. Gus waited eleven days for the part. His little girl, Dot, asked him every evening whether the corn was going to be too late. "I don't know, sweet pea," he told her. "But I know Who does. And I know He loves us, and He's never surprised." The part came on the twenty-fourth. Gus planted his whole field in two long days. That very weekend a hard frost came down out of the north, the latest anyone could remember. Up and down the valley, the young green corn turned black in the rows. Gus's seed was still safe in the ground, too new to have sprouted. His neighbors had to replant at great expense, and Gus, who had extra seed he no longer needed, gave his away to three of them. That fall Dot helped him bring in the best harvest the farm had seen in ten years. She rode on the fender of the repaired tractor, patting it like a horse. "Good job breaking," she told it. Gus laughed so hard he nearly drove into the ditch.

gh-all-things-work-together.title: The Winter Without Work
gh-all-things-work-together.body: The plant where Tom Ashby had worked for twenty-two years closed two weeks before Christmas. He came home with a cardboard box of his things and sat in the car in the driveway, unable to go inside and tell his wife. When he finally did, Grace held his hands at the kitchen table, and they prayed together, not a big prayer, just an honest one. They told Yahweh they loved Him, they were scared, and they belonged to Him. Then the hard winter began. The savings shrank. Tom applied for forty jobs and heard back from three. Some nights the fear came at him like a wind against the house, telling him his family was ruined. On those nights he would get out of bed, go to the kitchen, and say it again to the dark: "You are not surprised by this. You already know how it ends, and You love us." It did not make the winter warmer. But it kept him from panicking. While he waited, Tom fixed things for neighbors: a widow's leaking sink, a young couple's broken furnace, the church's ancient lawnmower. He had always been good with his hands. By March, people were calling him before they called anyone else. By June he had a truck with his name painted on the door. By the next winter he had hired two men from the closed plant who had been out of work even longer than he had. One night, coming home late, Tom stopped in the doorway of the kitchen where he and Grace had prayed that first night. He did not have to say anything. He just stood there and gave thanks.

gh-god-beyond-dimension.title: Ruby's Paper People
gh-god-beyond-dimension.body: Ruby was seven, and she had drawn her whole family on a long sheet of paper: Mom, Dad, baby Theo, the dog, and a lopsided house with smoke coming out of the chimney. She was showing it to her father when she asked a question that had been bothering her. "Daddy, where is Yahweh? Is He in the sky? If a rocket went really high, would it find Him?" Her father thought about it. Then he pointed at the paper. "Can the paper people see you?" Ruby giggled. "No, silly. They're flat. They only know left and right and up and down on the page." "If paper Dad walked all the way to the edge of the paper, would he find you?" "No. I'm not on the paper. I'm out here." "But you're holding the whole page, aren't you? And you could draw something right next to paper Dad, any time you wanted, anywhere you wanted." Ruby nodded slowly. Then her eyes went wide. "So Yahweh is like me, and we're the paper people?" "Something like that," her father said, smiling. "He's not far away up past the clouds. He's outside the whole page, holding it. Everything we know is inside what He made, and He keeps it all together. You can't reach Him by traveling, but He's closer to you than this paper is to your hand." Ruby looked at her drawing for a long time. Then she picked up her crayon, and in the corner of the page, very carefully, she drew a big hand holding the whole thing. She taped it to the refrigerator, and it stayed there for years.

gh-god-beyond-dimension.title: What the Telescope Could Not See
gh-god-beyond-dimension.body: Arthur Lindqvist spent forty years building bridges and thirty years as an amateur astronomer, and he believed only in what he could measure. He had looked deeper into the night sky than anyone in his town, and he liked to say, gently but firmly, that he had never seen any sign of Yahweh up there. The winter his granddaughter Elsie fell sick, Arthur sat beside her hospital bed every night. She was eight, small under the white blankets, and she asked him the question he had always dodged. "Grandpa, you look at stars. Did you ever see Yahweh?" Arthur opened his mouth to give his usual answer, and could not. Because on those long nights in that room, something had been happening that his instruments could not explain. He had felt a Presence. Not up past the ceiling, not out among the galaxies, but there, in the room, closer than the walls, as near as the air. A peace that held him the way a hand holds a cup. "No," he said slowly. "I never saw Him with the telescope. I think I was looking the wrong way. I thought He had to be far away, at the end of what I could measure. But I think He's outside the whole thing, Elsie, holding all of it together. Every star I ever looked at. Every beam I ever built. And this room too." Elsie smiled and fell asleep holding his finger. She recovered that spring. Arthur still went out to his telescope on clear nights. But now, before he looked up, he bowed his head, and he held his old certainties about what was possible much more loosely than before.

gh-fruit-no-law.title: Owen and the Apple Tree
gh-fruit-no-law.body: Owen was ten, and his little sister Bea could drive him to distraction. She knocked over his block towers. She sang the same song forty times. She followed him everywhere. Owen had decided to be patient with her, and he tried very hard. He clenched his fists and counted to ten. He made a chart. He even promised himself a candy bar every day he did not yell. He lasted until Wednesday. Then Bea poured juice on his library book, and he shouted so loudly that the neighbor's dog started barking. That weekend at his grandfather's farm, Owen sat under the old apple tree feeling miserable, and told Grandpa everything. Grandpa listened. Then he reached up and pulled down a ripe red apple. "Did this tree grunt and squeeze to make this?" he asked. Owen almost smiled. "No." "It just stays connected to its roots, and the apples come. You've been trying to squeeze out patience like toothpaste. Patience is fruit, son. It grows when you stay close to Jesus." So Owen tried something different. Every morning before school, he sat with his grandfather's old Bible for ten minutes and talked to Jesus about his day, and about Bea. He did not make any more charts. Slowly, without his quite noticing, something changed. When Bea knocked over his blocks, he laughed and built them again with her. When she sang, he sometimes sang along. One evening his mother found them asleep on the couch together, his arm around her shoulders. "There's no rule against that," his father whispered, smiling. And no one, anywhere, would ever have wanted to make one.

gh-fruit-no-law.title: Miss Crane's Rulebook
gh-fruit-no-law.body: Miss Crane ran Hollister Academy with a rulebook three inches thick. There was a rule for how to hold a pencil, a rule for how to walk in the hall, a rule for how loudly to laugh at lunch. She had written most of them herself, and she enforced every one. The children obeyed her, and they were afraid of her, and not one of them loved her. Miss Crane did not love them either, though she would not have said so. She was too tired. Keeping all those rules had worn her down to the bone, and every year she added new ones to stop the old troubles, and the troubles always found a way around them. One winter her own mother died, and Miss Crane, who had not prayed in decades, found herself on her knees in her empty apartment. She did not know what to say. She only knew she was empty. In the weeks that followed she began to go to a small church, and to read the Gospels, and to stay close to Jesus in a way she had never been taught. Something began to grow in her. She noticed a boy crying by the bike rack and, instead of writing him up, she sat down beside him and listened. She laughed at a joke in the lunchroom. She learned every child's name. By spring the teachers noticed that the halls were calmer than they had been in years. In June, Miss Crane took her rulebook home and tore out two-thirds of it. Nobody broke the rules that were left. Love had done for Hollister what no rulebook had ever managed, and there was no law in any book against the woman she had become.

gh-triumph-already-public.title: The Ruling on the Gate
gh-triumph-already-public.body: For two years the Delacroix family had been in a dispute with a neighbor over the lane that ran across their land to the county road. The neighbor, Mr. Stiles, insisted the lane was his and kept parking his tractor across it. There were letters, then lawyers, then a long day in court. In October the judge ruled: the lane belonged to the Delacroix family, plainly and finally, and Mr. Stiles was to keep it clear. The ruling was stamped and filed and printed in the county paper for everyone to see. A week later, the tractor was back across the lane. Twelve-year-old Marcel came running in. "Dad, he's doing it again! Are we going back to court?" His father smiled and went to the drawer. "No, son. We don't have to win this again. It's already won." He took out a copy of the ruling, walked down to the lane, and knocked on Mr. Stiles's door. He did not shout. He did not argue the case all over. He simply held up the paper and said, "The court has already decided this. I'm asking you to move the tractor." Mr. Stiles grumbled, read the ruling, and moved it. It never came back. That night at supper, Marcel's father said, "That's how it is with the cross too. Jesus already won, out in the open, where everybody could see. We don't fight the darkness like it's still undecided. We just hold up what He already did." Marcel thought about that for a long time. Then he asked if he could keep the copy of the ruling, and he pinned it above his bed.

gh-triumph-already-public.title: Lorraine's Shelf of Books
gh-triumph-already-public.body: Lorraine Mabry had a whole shelf of books about darkness. She had read about every kind of evil and every way it might attack a family, and she could talk for hours about the enemy's schemes. She meant well. She thought that if she understood the darkness well enough, she could finally beat it. But the more she read, the more afraid she became. She checked the locks three times a night. She prayed long, frantic prayers, as if she were holding a door shut against something huge. Her children grew anxious too. Her house felt like a place under siege. One evening an older woman from church, Mrs. Tolliver, came by with a pie and noticed the shelf. She ran her finger along the spines and was quiet a long time. Then she said, "Lorraine, honey, you're studying the losing team." Lorraine bristled. "I'm trying to understand what we're up against." "I know. But the fight you're preparing for was settled at the cross. Jesus stripped the darkness of its power out in the open, in front of everyone, and it's finished. You don't need to research a defeated enemy to defeat him again. You just need to stand in what Jesus already did." Lorraine sat down heavily. She had never once thought of it as finished. That week she boxed up the shelf and gave the books away. In their place she put her Bible and a hymnbook. She still prayed every night, but her prayers changed. They were shorter, quieter, full of thanks instead of panic. Within a month, her children had stopped asking whether the doors were locked. Within a year, she had forgotten to be afraid.

gh-will-worship-frees-no-one.title: Curtis and the Chart
gh-will-worship-frees-no-one.body: Curtis Bell had a temper, and he was determined to fix it. So he made a plan, and it was a very impressive plan. He woke at five every morning and took a cold shower. He gave up coffee. He ran three miles. He wrote down every irritation in a little notebook and rated it from one to ten. He made a color chart for the refrigerator, with a box for every hour of the day, and he checked off each hour he did not lose his temper. His neighbors admired his discipline. His brother asked for a copy of the chart. Curtis felt very serious and very strong. Then, on the twelfth day, his son Danny spilled a can of paint on the garage floor, and Curtis shouted so loudly that Danny cried and ran inside. Curtis stood there, red-faced, holding his pencil, and looked at his beautiful chart. Twelve days of perfect boxes, and nothing in him had changed at all. His wife came out and sat on the step beside him. "You've been grading yourself," she said gently. "You haven't been going to Jesus." Curtis wanted to argue, but he could not. All that effort had looked wise. It had only made him tired. That night he did not make a new chart. He knelt by the bed and told Jesus the truth: that he could not fix himself, and that he needed Him. Then he went to Danny's room and asked his forgiveness. The change came slowly after that, but it came, from the inside out. Months later, Danny spilled a glass of milk at supper. Curtis laughed and handed him a towel. The chart had long since gone in the trash.

gh-will-worship-frees-no-one.title: The Ladder in the Binder
gh-will-worship-frees-no-one.body: When Nadia's anxiety grew so heavy that she could barely leave the house, a friend gave her a binder from a seminar she had attended. Inside were forty steps to freedom, each one a condition to meet before the next: fasting on certain days, saying certain prayers a certain number of times, avoiding certain foods and colors and songs, writing out lists of every possible open door in her life. It looked thorough. It looked holy. Nadia threw herself into it with everything she had. For eight months she climbed the ladder. She fasted until she was faint. She recited the prayers until she knew them in her sleep. She checked and rechecked her lists. Every time she finished a step, she waited to feel free, and every time the fear was still there, sometimes worse, because now she was also afraid she had done a step wrong. One gray afternoon her grandmother found her on the kitchen floor with the binder open in her lap, crying. Grandmother Aziz did not read the binder. She simply closed it and set it aside. "Child," she said, "you have been trying to climb up to Jesus. But He came down to you. He is not at the top of a ladder. He is right here." Nadia looked at her through her tears. She had been so busy with the procedure that she had forgotten the Person. That evening she did something she had not done in eight months. She prayed without a script, simply, like a child, and told Jesus she was tired and needed Him. The fear did not vanish that night. But for the first time it began to loosen, and it kept loosening, until one spring morning she noticed it was gone.

gh-jesus-i-know-who-are-ye.title: The Baker Knows His Friends
gh-jesus-i-know-who-are-ye.body: Mr. Lazaro's bakery on Fifth Street was famous for its cinnamon rolls, and he was famous for giving them away. Every friend who came in got one free, warm from the oven, with a pat on the shoulder. One morning a boy named Kip, who was eleven and always hungry, had an idea. He marched up to the counter and announced, in his most grown-up voice, "Mr. Lazaro's friend, here for my roll." Mr. Lazaro leaned on the counter and looked at him kindly. "Well, now. I know my friends. I know Mrs. Delgado, who comes in every morning. I know Pastor Wells, who prays for my mother. But who are you?" Kip turned bright red. He had used the right words, but the baker did not know him at all. Just then the door jingled and Mrs. Delgado came in. Mr. Lazaro lit up, called her by name, asked about her knee, and had a roll in her hand before she reached the counter. Kip watched. Mrs. Delgado did not say any special words. She did not need to. She was known. Kip slunk out of the bakery, embarrassed. But the next day he came back, and this time he did not ask for anything. He asked if he could sweep the floor. He came back the next day, and the next, and he listened to Mr. Lazaro's stories about his village, and learned how to fold dough. By the end of the summer, when Kip walked in, Mr. Lazaro called out his name from the back of the shop before he had said a word. Kip's grandfather, hearing the story, laughed and said that was exactly how it worked with Jesus too.

gh-jesus-i-know-who-are-ye.title: The Prayer That Fell Flat
gh-jesus-i-know-who-are-ye.body: By twenty-five, Trent Holloway knew every right phrase. He had studied the great preachers. He could pray in a voice that filled a room, and he used the name of Jesus often and with force, the way he had heard it done. People began to call him when trouble came. He liked that. He liked it so much that, somewhere along the way, he stopped praying when no one was listening. His Bible stayed in the car. His mornings were for planning sermons, not for sitting with the Lord. He did not notice. The words still came out right. Then one night a family from church called him in a panic. Their teenage son was in terrible trouble, raging, frightened, and breaking things, and the house was full of a heaviness no one could explain. Trent drove over confidently. He stood in the living room and spoke every right word in his loudest voice, and the name of Jesus came out of his mouth like a password. Nothing happened. The heaviness did not move. If anything, the boy laughed at him, a cold laugh that went right through him, and Trent, shaken and ashamed, made an excuse and fled to his car. He sat in the driveway trembling. Then he called old Pastor Greer, who came within the hour. Greer did not shout. He sat on the floor beside the boy, prayed quietly like a man talking to a Friend he knew well, and the room grew still. Trent drove home and wept until dawn. He understood now. He had been using the name of Someone who did not know him. From that night on, he stopped seeking to be equipped and started seeking to be known.

gh-presence-is-the-liberty.title: Where the Fire Is
gh-presence-is-the-liberty.body: On the Pham family's first camping trip, eight-year-old Lucy spent the whole first evening on patrol. She had heard about bears and raccoons and snakes, and she was not going to let any of them sneak up on her family. She circled the tent with a flashlight. She checked under the picnic table. She peered into the dark trees until her eyes ached, and every snapping twig made her jump. She did not roast a single marshmallow. Her father finally called her over to the fire. "Lucy, come sit with me." "I can't," she said. "I'm guarding." He patted the log beside him. "Come here a minute." She sat down, stiff and watchful. The fire crackled. Its warmth spread over her hands and face. In the circle of its light she could see everything: her mother laughing, her brother's sticky face, the stars coming out overhead. Her father put his arm around her. "You know what, sweetheart? The animals don't like the fire. They stay away from it. You don't have to patrol the whole forest. You just have to stay close to where the fire is." Lucy thought about that. Then, slowly, she let her flashlight click off. She roasted four marshmallows, burned two of them, and laughed until her stomach hurt. Later, snug in her sleeping bag, she whispered to her father that it was like Jesus. "When I stay close to Him, I don't have to be scared all the time." Her father kissed her forehead. "That's exactly it," he said. "Being free is just staying where He is." She was asleep before he finished the sentence.

gh-presence-is-the-liberty.title: Dennis and the Morning Chair
gh-presence-is-the-liberty.body: Dennis Whitaker had been free of the bottle for six years, and he guarded that freedom like a soldier on a wall. He drove the long way home to avoid the liquor store. He kept a list of every place, every person, and every feeling that had ever led him back. He counted the days on a calendar and checked himself every night like a man inspecting a fence for breaks. He was free, but he was exhausted, and some nights the vigilance itself felt like a cage. His sponsor, an old man named Mr. Curran, listened to all of this one evening over coffee. Then he asked a question that surprised Dennis. "When do you feel most free?" Dennis thought about it. "Sunday mornings, I guess. In church. When we're singing." "Why do you think that is?" Dennis did not know. "Because He's there," Mr. Curran said. "You've been treating freedom like ground you took and have to keep defending. But where the Spirit of the Lord is, that's where the liberty is. It isn't a wall you guard. It's a place you stay." The next morning Dennis set an old armchair by his kitchen window. Before work, before the news, before anything, he sat in it with his Bible and a cup of coffee and simply spent time with the Lord. Some days he read. Some days he only sat. He kept doing it, morning after morning. He still drove carefully, and he still kept wise boundaries. But the wall-walking began to fade. A year later he realized he had not looked at his list in months. He had stopped patrolling. He was simply staying near.

gh-submit-then-resist.title: Standing Next to Mr. Ruiz
gh-submit-then-resist.body: All of fifth grade, a bigger boy named Brock had been taking Jamal's lunch money at the bike rack. Jamal had tried everything his cousins told him. He puffed out his chest. He practiced a tough voice in the mirror. One day he even shouted "Leave me alone!" as loud as he could, all by himself behind the gym, and Brock just laughed and took the money anyway. Jamal went home and told his grandmother. She did not tell him to get tougher. She asked him a question. "Have you told Mr. Ruiz?" Mr. Ruiz was the school principal, a kind man who knew every child by name. Jamal had not told him. He had been too proud. The next morning he went to the principal's office first thing and told the whole story. Mr. Ruiz listened, nodded, and said, "Thank you for coming to me. Let's walk out together this afternoon." So at three o'clock Jamal walked to the bike rack with Mr. Ruiz right beside him. When Brock came over, Jamal said exactly the same words he had shouted before: "Leave me alone." This time his voice was not even loud. But Brock looked at Jamal, then at Mr. Ruiz standing close behind him, and backed away fast. He never came back. That night, Jamal's grandmother explained that it works the same way with temptation and every dark thing. "You don't start by shouting at it," she said. "You start by going to Yahweh, and staying close to Him. Then when you say no, your no means something, because of Who is standing with you."

gh-submit-then-resist.title: Kneeling First
gh-submit-then-resist.body: Every night for three years, Leon Fitch fought the same battle. The card room on Fourth Street called to him, and he had lost his savings there twice. So every night he stood in his kitchen and fought it with everything he had. He gritted his teeth. He said no out loud. He threw his car keys across the room. Some nights it worked. Many nights it did not, and he would find himself walking down Fourth Street anyway, hating himself every step. One evening his old friend Carlos found him sitting on the curb outside the card room, head in his hands. They walked home together, and Carlos asked him what he did when the pull came. Leon described the battle: the teeth, the keys, the shouting. Carlos nodded slowly. "You're fighting with nothing behind you, brother. You're skipping the first step." "What first step?" "You've never once bowed. You keep trying to resist on your own, as if you're the one in charge. First you give yourself to Yahweh, all of you, every night, every morning. You draw near to Him. Then you resist, from there, with Him close. Saying no without bowing first is just shouting into the wind." Leon did not like hearing it. But that night, when the pull came, he did something he had never done. He knelt on his kitchen floor and gave himself to Yahweh, plainly, holding nothing back. He stayed there a long while, praying, until he felt the nearness of the Lord. Then he stood and said no. The pull did not vanish forever that night. But it left, and it left faster each time after, because now his no had Someone behind it. Two years later, Leon had his savings back.

gh-not-bondage-again.title: The Boy Who Asked to Open the Fridge
gh-not-bondage-again.body: When Tomas came to live with the Hartwells, he was eight years old and he had lived in five homes. In the first weeks, Mrs. Hartwell noticed strange things. He asked permission before opening the refrigerator, every single time. He hid crackers under his mattress. He tiptoed past the living room as if he might be sent away for making noise. One night she found him standing in the kitchen doorway at midnight, hungry, waiting for someone to tell him it was all right to get a glass of milk. Mrs. Hartwell knelt down in front of him. "Tomas," she said, "you're not a guest here. You're not a worker who has to earn his supper. The papers are signed. You're our son. This is your kitchen. You can open the fridge whenever you want." Tomas looked at her as if she had told him the moon was made of cheese. It took a long time. Some days he forgot and asked permission again, and she would just smile and say, "Son." But slowly, he changed. He started calling her Mom. He started walking into the kitchen after school and making himself a sandwich, humming. One Saturday he flung open the refrigerator door, grabbed the orange juice, and called out, "Mom, we're almost out of juice!" exactly the way a son does. Mrs. Hartwell had to step into the pantry for a moment so he would not see her cry. That Sunday the pastor said that everyone who belongs to Jesus has been adopted by the Father, and that sons do not have to keep asking whether they are still allowed in. Tomas nudged his new mother and whispered, "Like me and the fridge."

gh-not-bondage-again.title: Margaret Checks the Door
gh-not-bondage-again.body: Margaret Quill had grown up under a hard and fearful religion, where every Sunday was a test she might fail and every prayer felt like knocking on a door that might not open. In her thirties she met Jesus truly, and the freedom of it nearly undid her. She was a daughter, not a servant. She was home. For years she lived in that liberty with a light heart. Then, slowly, without quite noticing, the old fear crept back in through a side door. It did not come as fear. It came as carefulness. She began to wonder whether she had prayed enough that day. Whether she had read enough. Whether she had confessed every last thing. She began to come to the Lord's table with her shoulders hunched, like someone checking whether she was still on the guest list. One Sunday, as the bread was passed, she found herself unable to take it, sure that some forgotten sin had disqualified her. An old friend in the next seat, Ida Monroe, noticed her trembling hand. After the service Ida walked her to her car. "Margaret," she said quietly, "I watched you today. You looked like a servant waiting to be dismissed. You're not that anymore. You were set free once. Don't let anybody hand you that old yoke again, not even your own careful heart." Margaret sat in her car a long time after Ida left. She realized she had been renting her freedom by the week, as if it could be taken back. That night she prayed the way she had at the beginning, simply, as a daughter speaks to her Father. The next Sunday she took the bread with a steady hand, and she did not check the door again.

gh-keep-yourself-by-the-word.title: Clara's Index Cards
gh-keep-yourself-by-the-word.body: Clara was eleven when her Sunday school teacher gave every child a stack of blank index cards and a challenge: one verse a week, written by hand and carried in your pocket until you knew it by heart. Most of the kids lost their cards by Tuesday. Clara kept hers. Every night she read the week's card before bed. Every morning she read it on the bus. It never felt like much, just a few minutes, a little bit at a time. By spring she had a rubber-banded stack of thirty cards. Then came the day at school when a group of girls cornered her in the hallway and dared her to write something cruel about the new girl on the bathroom wall. Clara's heart pounded. She wanted them to like her. But right in that moment, a verse she had carried in her pocket for a week came back to her, clear as a bell, and she knew what to do. "No," she said. "I won't." She walked away and sat with the new girl at lunch. That night she told her mother what had happened. "I didn't even have to think," Clara said. "It was just there." Her mother smiled. "That's why you put it there before you needed it," she said. "You can't pull out of your pocket what you never put in." Then her mother asked the most important question: "And what did you do with it?" Clara thought. "I did what it said. The same day." "That's the other half," her mother said. Clara took out a fresh card that night and wrote the next verse. One more line. One more week. It was not much. It was enough.

gh-keep-yourself-by-the-word.title: Frank's Resolutions
gh-keep-yourself-by-the-word.body: Every January first for twenty years, Frank Mercer made a giant resolution. He would read the entire Bible in a month. He would pray an hour every morning. He would become, all at once, the man he knew he should be. And every year, by the second week of February, the resolution had collapsed, and Frank felt worse than if he had never started. By his fifties he had stopped trying. He sat in the back pew and felt like a failure. One spring he helped his neighbor, an old farmer named Mr. Abbot, plant a long row of fruit trees. Frank watched him water each sapling, a little at a time, morning after morning. "How long until they bear?" Frank asked. "Years," said Mr. Abbot. "You don't make a tree grow by yelling at it in January. You water it today. Then you water it tomorrow." He looked at Frank. "Same with a man's soul." Frank asked him what he meant. Mr. Abbot told him that he read one small passage from the Word every morning, chewed on it, and did one thing it said before supper. "I keep myself close to Him," he said. "And He keeps me. Both hands. He does His part, and I do mine." So Frank tried it. One passage. One obedience. The next day, the next. Nothing dramatic happened. But a year later he realized he had read more of the Word than in all his January sprints combined. Five years later his wife told him he was a different man. Frank did not feel arrived. He only felt the path getting brighter, a little more each morning.

gh-conviction-vs-condemnation.title: The Broken Model Ship
gh-conviction-vs-condemnation.body: Marcus was ten when he knocked his sister Elena's model ship off the shelf. She had spent all winter building it, every tiny mast and rope, and now it lay on the carpet in three pieces. Marcus felt sick. The feeling was sharp and specific: I did this, it was her ship, and I need to tell her. So he did. He knocked on her door, held out the pieces, and said, "I broke it. I'm so sorry. I'll help you fix it." Elena cried a little, then sighed, and the two of them spent the evening at the kitchen table with a tube of glue and a pair of tweezers. By bedtime the ship was back on the shelf, a little crooked, but whole. Elena hugged him and said it was fine. Marcus went to bed feeling clean. But the next afternoon, out of nowhere, a different feeling came. It was not sharp. It was foggy and heavy, and it said: You always ruin everything. You're a careless person. Nobody should trust you. It did not tell him to do anything. It just made him want to hide in his room. Marcus told his father about it at dinner. His father put down his fork. "Son, the first feeling, the one that sent you to your sister's door with the pieces, that was from the Lord. It was specific, it gave you something to do, and it brought you home. This second one is vague and it drives you away. That one isn't from Him. You already made it right. You're forgiven. You don't have to carry it again." Marcus thought about it. Then he went upstairs, looked at the crooked ship, and smiled.

gh-conviction-vs-condemnation.title: The Sentence Already Served
gh-conviction-vs-condemnation.body: Thirty years ago, when she was young and tired and angry, Corinne Walsh had said a cruel thing to her mother in a hospital room, and walked out, and her mother had died that night before Corinne could come back. In the weeks after, Corinne had wept and confessed it to the Lord with her whole heart, and she had known, truly known, that she was forgiven. But the guilt kept returning. It never came as a clear call to do something. It came as a heavy fog in the middle of the night, whispering that she was a terrible daughter, that she had always been selfish, that someone like her had no business praying. Every time it came, she stopped reading her Bible for a week. She stopped going to her women's group. She pulled away from everyone who loved her. One evening she finally told her pastor's wife, an older woman named Mrs. Bray. Mrs. Bray listened, then asked her a single question. "When this guilt comes, which way does it push you? Toward Jesus, or away from Him?" Corinne did not have to think. "Away. Always away." "Then it isn't the Holy Spirit," Mrs. Bray said gently. "When He convicts, it's specific, it gives you something to do, and it brings you home. You already did what He asked. You confessed. You were forgiven thirty years ago. This other voice is only dragging out a sentence Jesus already served for you. There is no condemnation left for you to carry." Corinne sat very still. Then she began to weep, but it was a different kind of weeping. That night the fog came again. This time she did not argue with it or hide from it. She simply answered it with what Jesus had already done, and went back to sleep.

gh-word-is-4d-fact.title: Flying Through the Cloud
gh-word-is-4d-fact.body: Grandpa Elias had flown small airplanes for forty years, and on Josie's twelfth birthday he took her up for her first flight. The morning was bright, the fields below were green and gold, and Josie pressed her nose to the window, delighted. Then, halfway home, they flew into a cloud. Everything went white. There was no ground, no sky, no up or down. After a minute Josie said, uneasily, "Grandpa, I think we're tipping. It feels like we're leaning way over to the left." Grandpa Elias tapped a round dial on the panel. "What does this say?" Josie looked. The little airplane on the dial was perfectly level. "But it feels like we're leaning," she said. "I know," he said calmly. "In a cloud, your body tells you all kinds of things that aren't true. Your feelings aren't lying on purpose, honey. They just can't see far enough in here. This instrument can. So I trust it over what I feel." A few minutes later they burst out of the cloud into sunshine, and the wings were exactly level, just as the dial had said. Josie let out a long breath. On the drive home, Grandpa told her that he flew his life the same way. "There are days when everything I can see and feel says one thing, and Yahweh's Word says another. When that happens, I don't throw out my eyes. I just remember that they only see part of the sky. His Word sees all of it, and it has never once been wrong. So I hold steady and keep flying." Josie thought about that for a long time. Then she asked when they could fly again.

gh-word-is-4d-fact.title: The Dry Year on the Bauer Farm
gh-word-is-4d-fact.body: The summer the rain stopped, Henry Bauer measured everything. He was a careful man, and he did not believe in pretending. He checked the rain gauge every morning and wrote it down: nothing, nothing, a tenth of an inch, nothing. He measured the creek as it dropped, then vanished. He kept honest books on the feed he would have to buy and the money he did not have. Every number he wrote said the same thing: the farm that had been in his family for ninety years was going under. His banker said so. His neighbors, selling off their herds one by one, said so. Henry did not argue with any of it. The numbers were real. But every night, after he closed his ledger, Henry opened his grandfather's Bible to the promises his family had stood on for three generations, promises from a Yahweh who had never once failed to keep one. "Both of these are true," he told his wife, Ilse, one night at the kitchen table. "The gauge is true. And He is truer. The gauge only sees this one summer. He sees the whole thing." So Henry kept working, and kept praying, and kept measuring honestly, and did not let the numbers have the last word. In September the rain still had not come. But a letter did, from a cousin in another state with a dairy operation and more hay than he could use, offering to ship it at cost and wait on payment. Then the church took up a collection. Then the bank, for reasons it never explained, extended the note. The Bauer farm did not go under. And the next spring, it rained.

gh-faithful-crown.title: The Trophy Nobody Wanted Early
gh-faithful-crown.body: The Hawks lost their first game nine to nothing, and their second eleven to one, and by October the other boys had mostly stopped coming to practice. Theo did not stop. He came when it rained and the field turned to soup. He came the Saturday his cousins went to the lake. He came the week a bigger boy called him Coach's Puppy and the whole bleacher laughed. His mother asked him once, gently, why he kept going to a team that never won. Theo shrugged. "Coach said he'd be there every practice till the last whistle. So I figured I would too." Coach Ferris never made speeches about it. He simply opened the gate at four o'clock, set out the cones, and ran drills with whoever showed up, sometimes three boys, sometimes only Theo. The season ended with one tie and no wins. At the little banquet in the church basement, the other parents expected nothing much. Then Coach Ferris stood, lifted a tall gold trophy from under the table, and said it was not for the best player or the top scorer. It was for the one who was still standing on the field when the season ran out. He did not mail it or set it on a chair. He walked down the long table and put it into Theo's hands himself. Theo held it the whole drive home. It was heavy, and it was his, and it had been promised, his mother realized, from the very first practice, to whoever would simply not quit.

gh-faithful-crown.title: Grandma Ruth's Last List
gh-faithful-crown.body: For fifty-one years Ruth Calloway kept a prayer list on the inside door of her kitchen cabinet. Names went on in pencil. When an answer came she drew a small star beside the name, and when the cabinet door filled up she started a new sheet and taped it over the old one. The years were not easy on her. She buried a husband, lost the house on Maple Street when the mill closed, and spent her last winter in a narrow bed by the window with an illness the doctors could slow but not stop. Her granddaughter Abby visited every Sunday and noticed something she could not explain. Ruth was not afraid. Her body was failing, her hands shook too hard to hold a pencil, and still every week she asked Abby to read the list aloud, and every week she prayed it, name by name, in a whisper. "Aren't you tired, Grandma?" Abby asked once. "Of course I am, honey," Ruth said. "But I gave the Lord my yes a long time ago. I am not taking it back on the last lap." She went home to Him on a quiet morning in March. When the family cleaned out the kitchen, Abby peeled back the sheets on the cabinet door, one by one, fifty-one years deep, and counted more stars than she could finish counting. On the newest sheet, at the very bottom, in Abby's own handwriting from that last Sunday, was one more line Ruth had asked her to add: Still faithful. Not afraid. Abby kept that sheet. She believes, with everything in her, that her grandmother was met at the door by the King Himself, and that He did not hand her a crown from a distance.

gh-overcome-throne.title: The Chair Beside the Head of the Table
gh-overcome-throne.body: In the Marsh family, every child learned carpentry the hard way, in their father's shop behind the barn, through two long years of sanding, measuring twice, and starting over. Sam had finished it. Now it was his little brother Jonah's turn, and Jonah was ready to quit by the third week. His dovetails gapped. His thumb was blue. He had ruined a good board of walnut and nobody had yelled, which somehow felt worse. One evening Sam found him sitting on the shop step with his face in his hands. Sam sat down beside him and held up his own left hand, where a pale scar crossed the knuckle. "That's from week three," he said. "I ruined two boards of walnut, not one. I wanted to quit too. Dad kept setting a new board in front of me, and I kept picking up the chisel." He stood and pulled Jonah up with him. "I walked this whole road already. I'll walk it with you." So Sam came out to the shop after supper, night after night, and stood beside his brother at the bench. The gaps closed slowly. The thumb healed. By the second harvest, Jonah had built a whole oak chair with his own hands. That Thanksgiving their father did something he had done only once before. He carried Jonah's chair to the head of the long table and set it beside his own, right next to Sam's. "There's room up here," he said, "for every one of mine who finishes." Jonah sat down slowly, the way you sit in a place you have earned and still cannot believe is yours. Sam just grinned at him across the gravy boat, like a brother who had known all along.

gh-overcome-throne.title: The Boy Who Kept a Bag Packed
gh-overcome-throne.body: Daniel came to the Whitakers at eleven years old with one duffel bag, and for the first year he never fully unpacked it. He had lived in four homes before theirs. In every one of them he had eventually done the thing that sent him away: hidden food under the mattress, slipped a twenty from a purse, run off for a night to prove he could. He fully expected to do it again here, and to be sent on again. Mr. Whitaker did not pretend the old habits were not real. When Daniel took money from the church offering plate that spring, Mr. Whitaker found out, sat him down, and made him return it in person to the pastor. Then he drove Daniel home, not to the agency office. "That's not who you are in this house," was all he said. Daniel fought it for two years. Some weeks he won and some weeks the old boy won. But slowly he began to look like the man at the head of the table: he told the truth when it cost him, he worked when he was tired, he stayed when he wanted to run. The night before the adoption hearing, Mrs. Whitaker found the duffel bag empty at last, folded flat on the closet shelf. In the judge's chambers the next morning, Mr. Whitaker signed his name and slid the pen across to Daniel. "Your turn, son." Daniel signed beneath him, the same last name. That evening there was a new chair at the dinner table, the one right beside his father's. Nobody had to tell Daniel what it meant. He had fought his way, with his father's help, into the family he now resembled, and the seat had been waiting the whole time.

gh-door-sup.title: Thursday Soup
gh-door-sup.body: When the Ndiaye family moved onto Birch Lane, Fatou noticed that the old man in the gray house never came out. His porch light was always on. His curtains were always closed. The neighbors said Mr. Lindgren had not opened his door to anyone since his wife passed three winters before. So on the first Thursday, Fatou's mother made a pot of peanut soup, ladled it into a jar, and sent Fatou across the street with it. Fatou knocked. Nobody came. She left the jar on the step with a note: We live across the street. We made too much. The next Thursday she knocked again, and again nobody came, though she was almost sure the curtain moved. Her mother would not let her leave the jar any other way. "We knock," she said. "We wait. We do not open his door for him. That handle is on his side." Week after week the jars went across and came back empty, washed, set neatly on the Ndiayes' step at dawn. Then, on the ninth Thursday, Fatou knocked and the bolt slid back. Mr. Lindgren stood there in a cardigan with a hole in the elbow, holding the jar from last week. "I have two bowls," he said, a little gruffly. "It seems wrong to eat good soup alone at a table built for two." So Fatou and her mother went in. They sat at a small round table by the window with the curtains finally open, and the three of them ate soup and bread while the light went gold across the floor. Mr. Lindgren laughed twice. On the walk home, Fatou realized they had been knocking for nine weeks to give him supper, and he had ended up giving them his.

gh-door-sup.title: The Father on the Stairs
gh-door-sup.body: When Marcus was nineteen he said terrible things to his father, packed a car, and left for a city four hours away. For six years he answered no calls. He moved twice so the letters would stop finding him. They found him anyway. Then one November evening there was a knock at his apartment door. Marcus looked through the peephole and his breath caught. His father stood in the hallway, grayer than he remembered, holding a paper sack that smelled of the meatloaf his mother used to make. Marcus did not open the door. He stood on his side of it with his hand flat against the wood. His father did not pound. He did not shout or try the handle. He knocked once more, softly, and said through the door, "I'm not here to fight, son. I'm here to eat with you. I'll be on the stairs." Marcus heard him sit down. An hour passed. Then two. Marcus paced his small kitchen and argued with himself, rehearsing every reason he had to stay angry. Each reason felt thinner than the last. Near midnight he opened the door. His father was still on the top step, the sack on his knees, cold now. He stood slowly and did not step forward until Marcus said, almost in a whisper, "Come in, Dad." They warmed the meatloaf in a skillet and ate it at the counter on mismatched plates. They did not settle six years in one night. But they sat at the same table, and when his father left at two in the morning, Marcus asked him to come back next Sunday. All those years, Marcus realized later, the man had never once forced the lock. He had only kept knocking, and kept a supper waiting on the other side.

gh-nothing-unclean.title: The Guards at the Hive
gh-nothing-unclean.body: Ivy spent the whole summer at her grandfather's farm watching his bees, and the thing that fascinated her most was not the honey. It was the guards. A few bees always stood at the little entrance board of each hive, turning and checking every bee that landed. Most of them walked right in. But one afternoon Ivy watched a strange yellow wasp try to slip through, and the guards were on it in an instant, and out it went. "Why are they so strict, Grandpa?" she asked. "That wasp only wanted a little honey." Her grandfather lifted a frame dripping gold in the sunlight. "Because a hive is only as clean as its door, Ivy. Let one robber in, and the next week there are fifty, and they carry off everything the family built. Let one sick stranger in, and the whole colony can fall. The guards are why this honey is still good." Ivy chewed her lip. "How do they know who belongs?" "By scent," he said. "Every bee that belongs to this hive carries the smell of home on her. The guards know their own." Ivy thought about that for a long while, sitting on the upturned bucket with her chin in her hands. Then she asked, very quietly, whether she would be let into the City where Yahweh lives, the one Grandpa talked about at supper. Her grandfather set down the frame and knelt beside her. "Not because you never made a mistake, sweet girl. Because your name is written down with the Lamb, and you carry the smell of His house on you now. So live like it." That evening Ivy gave back the cookie she had taken without asking. It seemed the kind of thing a bee from a good hive would do.

gh-nothing-unclean.title: The Gardener Who Was Written In
gh-nothing-unclean.body: For three summers the Elm Street community garden was ruined by the same man. Everyone knew it was Royce. He climbed the fence at night, pulled up tomatoes, stole tools, and once poured salt along the bean rows out of plain spite. People stopped planting. Weeds took the beds. Finally old Mrs. Abernathy, who had started the garden forty years earlier, built a proper gate with a lock and hung a ledger beside it. Only gardeners whose names were written in the book would get a key. The neighbors cheered. Nothing that wrecks a garden would get back in. One gray April morning Royce himself was standing at the gate, hands in his pockets, looking at the ground. "I want in," he said. "I know what I did. I can't pay it back. I don't have it." Mrs. Abernathy studied him for a long time. Then she said, "The damages were paid last fall. I paid them. Every tool and every seed." She opened the ledger, wrote his name in her careful hand, and pressed a key into his palm. Royce stared at it as if it might burn him. "Why would you do that?" "Because the gate is not there to keep people like you out," she said. "It's there to keep the thing you used to do out. The man who did that is not the man standing here." Royce came every day that summer. He weeded the beds he had poisoned. He fixed the fence he used to climb. By August the neighbors had planted again, and the garden was greener than anyone could remember. And the man who locked the gate every evening, checking every latch twice, was Royce, whose name was written in the book, and who lived like it.

gh-word-of-testimony.title: Grandma Pearl's Breakfast Bible
gh-word-of-testimony.body: Every morning before the coffee finished, Grandma Pearl sat at the kitchen table with her worn Bible and a bowl of oatmeal, and her grandson Nate learned early not to talk to her until she had finished both. "I'm eating twice," she told him. "Once for my body and once for the rest of me." Nate thought it was just a grandma saying, until the spring of the bake sale. The church youth group had raised nearly four hundred dollars, and when the count came up forty short, a woman named Mrs. Tibbs let it be known around town that Pearl had been the last one holding the cash box. The talk spread quickly. Nate was furious. Pearl was not. When the pastor called, she simply told him what happened: she had handed the box, sealed, to the boy who helped her count it, and he could say so. Then she went back to her oatmeal. What surprised Nate was how quickly the rumor died. Nobody believed it. The checkout lady at the grocery laughed out loud. The mailman shook his head. "Pearl Haskins once drove twelve miles to return a dime I gave her by mistake," he said. Her whole life said one thing, and it said it louder than the rumor. The missing forty dollars turned up a week later, folded inside a cookie tin. At the next service, Pearl stood to thank the young man who had helped her count, by name, and the women who had baked, by name. Then she lifted her hands toward Yahweh and gave Him the rest. Nate understood something that morning. His grandmother's words and his grandmother's life had been reading off the same page for so long that there was nothing left for anyone to argue with.

gh-word-of-testimony.title: What the Man in the Back Row Said
gh-word-of-testimony.body: The town council meeting was supposed to be simple: a vote on letting the old fire hall become a youth center. Curtis Boyd stood to speak for it, because he had spent the last six years coaching boys from the trailer park on Saturdays. He had barely said his name when a man in the back row stood up. "Before anybody listens to him," the man said loudly, "you should know who he is." And he told them. The arrests twenty years back. The drinking. The family business Curtis had run into the ground. The months he had spent in the county jail. Every word of it was true. The room went cold and silent. Curtis gripped the edge of the podium. Then he did something nobody expected. He nodded. "That's all true," he said. "I was that man, and I am not going to stand here and pretend I wasn't. But I'll tell you what happened since." And he told them plainly. How he had sat in that jail with a Bible a chaplain left him and read it like a starving man eats. How Jesus had washed what Curtis could never wash on his own. How he had worked six years to pay every creditor back. How an old deacon named Mr. Pruitt had driven him to work every morning when he had no license and no friends. "Whatever good I've done, give Mr. Pruitt the credit, and give the Lord the glory," he said. "I'm only what was paid for." Then he sat down. The man in the back row had nothing more to say. Neither did anyone else, until Mr. Pruitt, eighty years old, stood up slowly and said, "I'll vouch for every word." The vote passed eleven to nothing. What had been thrown at Curtis to silence him had only given him the floor.

gh-judge-comes-with-reward.title: Two Faces at the Window
gh-judge-comes-with-reward.body: When Grandpa Elias left for his three-week trip across the ocean, he gave each of his grandchildren one row of the vegetable garden to tend. "When I come back," he said, tapping his hat, "I'll see what you did with it." Lucy watered her beans every morning before school. She pulled weeds in the heat and staked her peas when the wind knocked them flat. Her cousin Brody meant to, but there was always a game to finish or a bike to ride, and by the second week his row had disappeared under thistles. On the last afternoon, a car turned into the long gravel drive. Lucy saw it first. She shrieked and ran to the window, then out the door, her braids flying. Brody saw it too, and his stomach dropped, and he slipped around the back of the house to hide behind the shed. Grandpa climbed out holding a paper sack in each hand. He walked straight down to the garden, where Lucy was already pulling him by the sleeve to see her beans, fat and green on the vine. He knelt in the dirt, looked a long time, and laughed out loud. Then he handed her the first sack: a little brass watering can with her name stamped on it. He walked to the next row and stood quietly over the thistles. "Brody," he called, not angrily. "Come out. I brought one for you too, and some seeds. We'll start over together tomorrow." Brody came out slowly, cheeks red. That night at supper, Lucy could not stop smiling. She had spent three weeks watching the road, she realized, not out of fear, but because she could not wait for him to see.

gh-judge-comes-with-reward.title: The Chair by Mr. Benson's Window
gh-judge-comes-with-reward.body: All his life, Walter Benson had been afraid of the end of the world. As a boy he had heard preachers describe the Day of the Lord as a great courtroom, and he had pictured himself standing alone in it, every wrong he ever did read aloud while he trembled. He tried to be good out of that fear. He tithed out of that fear. At seventy-eight he still could not hear a sermon about the return of Jesus without his hands going cold. That winter his granddaughter Mae moved in to help him, and she began to read to him in the evenings. Not the parts he dreaded, but all of it, the whole long story of a King who had paid for His family and was coming back for them. One night she stopped and asked him a simple question. "Grandpa, do you love Him?" "Of course I do." "Then why are you so scared to see Him?" Walter had no answer. He thought about it for days. He thought about the men he had worked beside at the mill for forty years, how they had dreaded the plant inspector, while he, who did his work honestly, had always been glad to see the man come, because the inspector brought the bonus checks. Slowly something turned over in him. The Judge he feared was the same One he loved, and He was coming with the reward in His own hand. In early spring Mae noticed that her grandfather had moved a second chair beside his window, facing the road. "For when He comes," Walter said, a little embarrassed. "I'd like to see Him first." He sat there every morning after that, his coffee in his hands, no longer bracing for a summons, but watching the road for a Friend.

gh-god-not-colorblind.title: The Notices Lucia Could Not Read
gh-god-not-colorblind.body: Grace was proud of how she treated the new girl. "I don't even notice that Lucia's different," she told her mother. "I treat her exactly like everybody else." Her mother smiled, but asked a question. "Did you know Lucia's mother doesn't read English yet?" Grace did not know. She had not asked. The next week she found out what it meant. Every notice from school went home in English: the field trip form, the picture day money, the note about early dismissal. Lucia kept missing things. She came on picture day in her old sweater. She stood alone at the curb on the half day, waiting an hour for a ride that did not know to come. Everyone treated her exactly the same, and exactly the same was leaving her out. So Grace asked. She sat beside Lucia at lunch and asked about her family, her town, her grandmother's songs, the language they spoke at home. Lucia lit up. She talked more that day than she had in a month. That weekend Grace and her mother helped Lucia's mother write a short list of school words in both languages, and Grace began carrying the notices to Lucia's house and reading them out loud while Lucia translated. At the spring program at church, the children's choir sang one hymn in four languages, one verse each, and Lucia led the Spanish verse in a clear, bright voice. Grace stood beside her, not singing, just listening. It sounded, she thought, the way Yahweh must like it to sound, every voice its own, nobody pretending not to hear the difference, and all of them singing to the same King.

gh-god-not-colorblind.title: What Elder Harold Finally Asked
gh-god-not-colorblind.body: Harold Pennington had been an elder at Cedar Creek Church for twenty-two years, and he said often, with real pride, that he treated every person who walked through those doors exactly the same. "I don't see where a man comes from," he liked to say. "I just see a brother." So he was puzzled when Samuel Osei, a young father who had been coming for two years, quietly stopped attending the men's breakfast. Harold went to see him. Samuel was polite but tired. Finally he said, "Mr. Pennington, every time I walk in, somebody asks if I'm visiting. Two years, and I'm still visiting. Last month someone asked me to help carry tables and asked the man beside me to pray. And you all say you don't see any difference. But I live inside the difference every day." Harold started to defend himself and stopped. "Tell me," he said instead. So Samuel told him. About his grandmother, who had come to this very town as a young woman and been turned away from a church just down the road. About the jokes he still heard at work. About the extra questions at the bank. Harold listened for two hours and did not interrupt once. Driving home, he understood that his not seeing had been a kind of not looking. The next Sunday he asked Samuel to stand and share his family's story with the whole congregation, and to lead the closing prayer. Samuel's daughters sat in the front row, beaming. Afterward the oldest members lined up to shake his hand, and one of them, a woman of ninety, wept and said she remembered his grandmother. Harold watched it all and thought of the great gathering before the throne, where every tribe is named and none is erased.

gh-yahweh-gets-both.title: Thank the Baker, Not the Bread
gh-yahweh-gets-both.body: Felix was seven when he asked his grandmother the big question, right in the middle of breakfast. "Why do we only worship Yahweh? Wouldn't it be nicer to worship lots of things?" Grandma Ines set down her coffee and reached for the loaf of bread on the table. "Who made this?" "Mr. Duarte at the bakery." "Do we thank him?" "Yes. You always say thank you." "Do we bow down to him?" Felix giggled. "No!" "Why not?" He thought hard. "Because he's just a man. He's nice, but he's just a man." Grandma Ines nodded and pointed out the window, where the morning sun was pouring over the wheat field next door. "What about the sun? It grew the wheat. Should we thank the sun?" Felix frowned. "The sun doesn't know it's doing anything." "That's right. So Mr. Duarte gets a thank you, because he really did the baking, but he isn't worthy of worship. And the sun is beautiful, but it didn't decide to do anything, so it can't even get a thank you." She leaned closer. "Now who made the wheat, and the sun, and Mr. Duarte's hands, and your hands, and the very morning?" Felix's eyes went wide. "Yahweh." "He did all of it, so He gets the thanks. And He is good all the way through, so He gets the worship. Nobody else gets both, Felix. Nobody else even qualifies." Felix was quiet for a while. Then he bowed his head, right there over the bread, and thanked Yahweh first, and then, because it was only right, he ran down the street after breakfast and thanked Mr. Duarte too.

gh-yahweh-gets-both.title: The Sculptor and the Statue
gh-yahweh-gets-both.body: Old Anselm had carved the statue of the Harvest Woman for the village square when he was a young man, and it was the best work he ever did. Her face was calm, her arms full of wheat, her eyes turned toward the hills. For years people simply admired her. Then came three hard years of drought, and slowly something changed. Someone left a flower at her feet. Then a candle. Then whole families came at dusk to kneel before her and beg for rain. They spoke of her as though she could hear. When a good harvest finally came, they hung garlands on her and held a festival in her name. Anselm, now bent and white-haired, watched it all from his doorway with a heavy heart. On the night of the festival he climbed onto the low wall beside the statue, and the crowd grew quiet out of respect for the old man. "I made her," he said, laying his hand on the cold stone. "I know every chisel mark. She has never heard a single one of your prayers. She did not send the rain. She cannot hold what you are trying to give her." Murmurs rose. Anselm raised his voice. "Thank me for the carving if you like, though my hands were a gift too. But do not kneel to anything I made. Kneel to the One who made me, and the stone, and the rain, and the hills she's looking at. He is the only One who did the work and is worthy of the worship both." Some walked away angry. But many stayed, and the next morning the garlands were gone, and the square was empty, and the little church at the end of the road was full.

gh-spirit-formed-and-returns.title: The Name Inside the Violin
gh-spirit-formed-and-returns.body: When Clara turned eleven, her grandmother let her borrow the family violin, the one that had come over on a ship with Clara's great-great-grandfather. It was old and dark and glossy, and it sang in a way the school violins never did. By spring Clara was playing so well that her teacher entered her in the regional festival, and she won first place. She came home glowing. "I'm a natural," she announced at supper. "It's just in me." Her grandmother smiled and asked her to bring the violin to the table. She tilted it gently toward the lamp so Clara could see through the little curved openings in the top. There, on a yellowed paper label inside, in faded ink, was a name Clara had never noticed: not hers, not her grandmother's, but the name of the man who had carved it, a hundred and forty years earlier. "That music is real, Clara, and it is beautiful," her grandmother said. "But somebody made the thing that makes it. And someday you'll hand it back." Clara turned the violin over in her hands, quiet now. "And the part of you that plays," her grandmother went on, softer, "that was made too. Yahweh formed it inside you before you ever picked up a bow. It's on loan. It's precious. It's going home someday." Clara did not feel smaller after that. Oddly, she felt steadier. She practiced harder than ever, but she no longer had to be the source of everything. When she played at church that Easter, she closed her eyes and played for the One whose name was written on the inside of her.

gh-spirit-formed-and-returns.title: Going Home to the One Who Made Her
gh-spirit-formed-and-returns.body: In his last year of college, Jordan came home talking about the spark. A teacher had told him that every person carried a little piece of the divine inside, and that if he looked deep enough within himself, he would find that he was, in some way, becoming divine himself. It made him feel enormous. It also made him tired in a way he could not explain, as if he were always being asked to generate light from nothing. That winter his grandmother Esther grew very weak, and the family gathered at her bedside. Jordan sat with her in the afternoons. One day he tried to explain the spark to her. Esther listened patiently, her thin hand in his. When he finished, she smiled. "Oh, honey," she said. "I'm not a piece of anything. I'm something He made. He formed my spirit, the same as He laid down the mountains, and everything I ever understood came from Him too. In a little while I'm going back to Him. That's not small. That's the best thing that can be said about a person." Jordan felt tears come up that he had not expected. She did not seem tired at all, though her body was failing. She seemed rested. She went home quietly two weeks later, with a hymn playing low in the room. At the graveside, Jordan found himself thinking that he had spent a year trying to become something, while she had spent ninety years simply being someone's, and going home. He did not have to manufacture a soul. He only had to steward the one he had been given. For the first time in a long time, the tiredness lifted.

gh-eyes-opened-by-prayer.title: Owen and the Storm at Grandma's
gh-eyes-opened-by-prayer.body: At school that week, a boy named Trevor had told Owen about a trick for seeing spirits. You turned off all the lights, said certain words into a mirror, and waited. Trevor swore it worked. Owen did not try it, but he could not stop thinking about it, and on the weekend at Grandma June's farm, when a thunderstorm rolled in after dark and the power went out, the thought came back with teeth. He lay in the spare bed with his heart pounding, sure that something unseen was in the room. He crept down the hall and found Grandma June sitting calmly in her rocking chair by a single candle.
