When it was her turn, she climbed onto the beam and fixed her eyes on the bright exit sign at the far end of the gym, and every time her mind started to drift toward her own feet, she thought of that word. She did not fall once. She did not even think about the judges. Afterward Mrs. Tran hugged her and asked what had changed. Lucy held up her wrist and grinned.

gh-stand-on-word.title: The Hardware Store on Main
gh-stand-on-word.body: For thirty years, Victor's little hardware store had stood on Main Street, the kind of place where the owner knew which washer fit your faucet. Then a huge company built an enormous store at the edge of town, and the trouble began. Their prices undercut his. Their lawyers sent letters claiming his sign was too close to the road. Someone wrote cruel things about him online, calling him a crook and a has-been. Victor stopped sleeping. He spent his nights rehearsing his fear, imagining every way it could all fall apart. The more he looked at the threat, the bigger it grew, until it filled the whole sky. One night his wife found him at the kitchen table with his head in his hands. She put a Bible in front of him and said, "You've been looking at the wind, Victor." He knew what she meant. He had been looking at himself, at his losses, at the company and the critics. He had not been standing on anything but his own worry. So Victor started each morning in the Word before he opened the shop. He prayed for the people who wrote cruel things. He kept his prices honest and his service kind. When the lawyers' letters came, he answered them truthfully and calmly and did not panic. He made a point of decreasing, of letting his customers hear more about Yahweh's faithfulness than about Victor's troubles. The letters stopped. The online lies faded because his customers answered them. Three years later, the enormous store closed, and Victor's little shop on Main Street was still standing, because the ground he had stood on was never his own.

gh-sheep-voice.title: Grandma's Whistle
gh-sheep-voice.body: Grandma Rose had a whistle that nobody else in the world could make. It went up, then down, then up again, like a bird asking a question. She had whistled it to her children, and now she whistled it to her grandchildren, Ava and little Ben, every day of their lives: to call them in for supper, to find them in the backyard, to wake them gently from naps. One Saturday she took them to the big city park for the spring festival. It was crowded with thousands of people, music, food stands and balloons. Ava and Ben wandered off after a juggler and suddenly realized they could not see Grandma anywhere. Ben's lip started to tremble. A man nearby noticed. "Are you lost? Come with me," he said, smiling, holding out his hand. "I'll take you to your grandmother." But something in his voice was wrong. It was friendly, but it was not her voice, and the children had never heard it before. Ava took Ben's hand and stepped back. "No, thank you," she said, the way their mother had taught them. Just then, over all the noise of the festival, they heard it: up, down, up again. Both of them turned at the same instant and ran straight through the crowd to Grandma Rose, who was standing on a bench waving her hat. That night, tucking them in, she told them that Jesus is a Shepherd, and His sheep learn His voice the same way. "You knew my whistle because you've heard it every day since before you could walk," she said. "That's how you'll learn His voice too. Every day."

gh-sheep-voice.title: The Voice That Sounded Wise
gh-sheep-voice.body: Hannah went away to college at eighteen, and in her second year she joined a discussion group led by a gifted and charming teacher. He spoke beautifully. He quoted poets. He told the students that they were the authors of their own truth, that every path led to the same light, and that the faith they had grown up with was a childish story they could now outgrow. The other students hung on his every word. Hannah wanted to as well. He made her feel clever and grown up. But every week, when she walked back to her dorm, she felt a small ache, as if a song she loved had been played slightly off-key. She could not have argued with him point by point. He was far more educated than she was. She only knew that his voice did not sound like the Voice she had been hearing in the Word every morning since she was a little girl, when her father read to her at breakfast. One night she sat on her bed and read from the Gospel of John until midnight, and the difference became plain. The teacher's words were eloquent, but they were a stranger's words. The words on the page were her Shepherd's, and she had known them longer than she had known her own handwriting. She had been chosen and known by Him before she was born, and her heart recognized Home. Hannah stopped going to the group. She did not need to win the argument. She simply knew which Voice she belonged to, and the other one no longer pulled at her. Years later she led a Bible study on that same campus.

gh-closet.title: The Laundry Room
gh-closet.body: Nadia had five children, a part-time job and a house that never once got quiet. There was always someone hungry, someone crying, someone who could not find a shoe. For years she tried to pray in the middle of the noise and gave up, frustrated. Then one winter she found the one place in the house where nobody ever followed her: the laundry room. Nobody wanted to go in there, because if they did, they might be asked to fold something. So every morning at five-thirty, before the house woke up, Nadia carried her coffee and her Bible into the laundry room, shut the door, sat on an upside-down bucket between the washer and the dryer, and prayed. She did not pray fancy prayers. Nobody was listening but the Father. She told Him what she was afraid of, what she was grateful for, and what she did not know how to handle. Then she read and waited, and some mornings she felt Him teaching her things she had not known. Nobody knew about the bucket. But her family began to notice something. She did not yell as much. She laughed more. When her oldest son got into trouble at school, she handled it with a calm that surprised even her. Her neighbor asked her one day how she stayed so patient with five children. Nadia laughed and said it was the laundry room. Her neighbor thought she was joking. Her youngest daughter, though, started following her in at five-thirty. Now there are two buckets in the laundry room, and every morning, before the house wakes up, mother and daughter sit there together with the Father who sees in secret.

gh-closet.title: The Man Who Prayed on the Street Corner
gh-closet.body: Deacon Harold was known for his prayers. At church dinners, at funerals, at the opening of the town fair, someone always asked him to pray, and Harold always did, in a strong voice with grand words that made people nod. He loved it. Somewhere along the way he had stopped praying anywhere no one could hear him. When he was alone, he found he had nothing to say. Then his wife fell ill, and the grand words dried up. Standing at the hospital bedside, Harold opened his mouth and nothing came. There was no audience to perform for, only his wife, sleeping, and the beeping of the machines. He walked out to his truck in the dark parking lot and sat behind the wheel, and for the first time in many years he prayed with no one listening. It was not eloquent. He wept and said he was afraid. He said he did not know how to pray when nobody was watching. And in that unwitnessed hour, something happened that had not happened at any church dinner. He felt the Father near. He felt himself being taught, gently, how small and honest a real prayer could be. From then on, Harold went out to his truck every morning before dawn, shut the door, and met with the Father in secret. His wife recovered slowly. When people asked him to pray at church, his prayers had become shorter and quieter, and something in them made people weep. Harold never told anyone about the truck. But everyone could see that the man who prayed in public had finally learned to pray in private, and the reward was showing openly.

gh-feed-sheep.title: Miss Ada's Chain
gh-feed-sheep.body: When Miss Ada was eighty-two, the children at Grace Fellowship made her a paper chain for her birthday, and it reached all the way around the fellowship hall. Each link had a name written on it, and the children had a story to explain it. Sixty years before, Miss Ada had taught a Sunday school class of four boys in a borrowed basement. One of them, a fidgety boy named Calvin, had never forgotten the way she opened the Word to them each week like it was a letter from Home. When Calvin grew up, he taught a class of his own. One of his students was a quiet girl named Lorraine, who later taught a class of teenagers. One of those teenagers was Mr. Bishop, who now taught the very children who had made the chain. So the first link said Ada. The next said Calvin. Then Lorraine, then Mr. Bishop, then over a hundred children's names. At the very end of the chain was a link with crooked letters that said Toby. Toby was six. He had added himself that morning because, he announced proudly, he had taught his baby sister the story of the lost sheep. Miss Ada laughed until she cried. She had taught four boys in a basement and had no idea what would come of it. She had only done what she was asked, out of love for Jesus, passing on what she had received to people who would pass it on again. The chain was still growing. Miss Ada took the last link, Toby's, and held it up so everyone could see. Then she asked Toby to come show her how he had told the story.

gh-feed-sheep.title: Three Times He Asked
gh-feed-sheep.body: After forty years as a machinist, Walter retired and did not know what to do with himself. His wife had gone Home two years earlier, his children lived far away, and his days had no shape. He went to church and sat in the back and went home again. He felt that his useful life was over. One Sunday the pastor preached on the morning by the sea when Jesus asked Peter the same question three times, and three times told him what to do with the answer. Walter went home and could not stop thinking about it. That night, in his empty kitchen, he felt the question pressed on his own heart, three times, quietly. Did he love the Lord? He did, more than anything. Then what was he doing with it? The next week Walter told the pastor he would like to help, though he did not know how. The pastor introduced him to three young men from the neighborhood who had no fathers and no faith, but who needed jobs. Walter taught them to run a lathe in his garage. And while they worked, he taught them what he had been taught, line by line, from the worn Bible his own father had given him. He fed them lunch on Saturdays and the Word every day. Two of them came to faith. One of them, years later, began teaching young men in his own garage. Walter lived to see it. He said that in all his years as a machinist, he had never made anything that lasted like that. The Lord had asked him three times what he would do with his love, and he had finally answered by feeding the sheep.

gh-filled-righteousness.title: The Hungriest Girl in Seventh Grade
gh-filled-righteousness.body: Rosa was always hungry, her brothers liked to say. She was hungry for pancakes, for library books, for knowing how things worked. But the winter she turned twelve, she discovered a new hunger. Her grandmother gave her a Bible with her name stamped on the cover, and Rosa started reading it before bed. At first it was out of duty. Then it was out of curiosity. Then, to her surprise, it was because she wanted to. She wanted to know what was right, what Yahweh loved, how He wanted people to treat one another. She found herself reading by flashlight after lights out, the way she used to read adventure stories. That hunger changed the way she acted at school. When her friends started teasing the new girl from another country, Rosa sat with the new girl at lunch instead. When a classmate offered her the answers to a math test, she said no thanks and studied harder. Some of her friends called her a goody-goody, and for a few weeks she ate lunch with only the new girl for company. But she did not feel empty. That was what surprised her most. She felt full, as if something inside her had been fed. By spring, the new girl had become her best friend, and two of the girls who had teased her started sitting with them, too. Rosa told her grandmother all about it. Her grandmother just smiled and said that was how Yahweh answers that kind of hunger. Rosa thought about that. She had expected to be hungry forever. Instead she was filled, and the more she ate, the more there was.

gh-filled-righteousness.title: The Inspector Who Would Not Sign
gh-filled-righteousness.body: Thomas had been a building inspector for nineteen years when the biggest developer in the city asked him to sign off on a new apartment tower. The paperwork was perfect. The building was not. Thomas walked the site himself and found the fire exits too narrow and the wiring cheaper than the plans said. He refused to sign. The developer was patient at first. Then he was not. Thomas received a phone call suggesting that a man with three children should think about his future. His supervisor asked him to reconsider. When he would not, he was moved to a desk in a basement office, then quietly let go. His neighbors heard rumors that he had been fired for being difficult. Some stopped waving. It was the hardest year of his life. His family lived on his wife's salary and on groceries left on the porch by people from church. And yet Thomas found something he had not expected. He was not bitter. He was not ashamed. He had done what was right, and he knew it, and that knowledge fed him like bread. He prayed more that year than he ever had, and Yahweh was near. He was happy, in a way the rumors could not touch. Two years later, an engineer who had heard the story came forward, and the city ordered the tower repaired before anyone moved in. A newspaper ran a small article about the inspector who would not sign. A different city hired Thomas to train new inspectors. On his first day he told them that doing right might cost them, and that the cost was not a sign of failure. It was simply the price, and the filling came with it.

gh-word-framed-worlds.title: The Name in the Corner of the Game
gh-word-framed-worlds.body: Isaac's father wrote computer games for a living, and for Isaac's tenth birthday he made one just for him. It was a whole little world on the screen: rolling hills, a river with fish that jumped, a village with a baker and a blacksmith, and weather that changed from sun to snow. Isaac played it for weeks. He explored every cave. He learned that the river always flowed east and that the fish only jumped at sunset, and he started explaining these rules to his friends as if they were simply the way things were. One day his friend Marcus asked who made the rules. Isaac shrugged. "Nobody. That's just how the world works." That evening his father showed him a secret. In the bottom corner of the map, behind a waterfall, there was a little stone with letters carved into it: Made by Dad, for Isaac. Isaac stared. Of course. The river did not flow east by accident. The fish jumped at sunset because his father had decided they should. Every rule in that world had been written by someone standing outside it, before Isaac ever pressed start. Lying in bed that night, Isaac looked out his window at the real stars and thought about it. His mother always said that Yahweh had made everything there is, and that He was there before any of it. Isaac had always thought that was just a nice thing people said. Now it seemed like the most obvious thing in the world. The next morning at breakfast he thanked his father for the game. Then, before he ate, he thanked Yahweh for the stars.

gh-word-framed-worlds.title: The Astronomer's Last Lecture
gh-word-framed-worlds.body: Professor Eleanor Marsh had spent fifty years studying the stars. She had measured the distances between galaxies and the exact balance of forces that kept them from flying apart. She knew better than almost anyone how finely the universe was tuned, how a hair's difference in a hundred numbers would have left nothing at all. And for fifty years she had told her students it was a happy accident. She admired the design and never once named a Designer. In her final year of teaching, her granddaughter Lily came to stay with her. Lily was eight, and one clear night Eleanor took her up to the observatory on the roof and let her look through the great telescope at a spiral galaxy. Lily gasped. Then she asked the simplest question in the world: "Who made it, Grandma?" Eleanor opened her mouth to give her usual answer about chance, and found that she could not say it to a child. The words would not come. She looked at the galaxy, at the precise, impossible order she had spent her life measuring, and realized that the design had been telling her the truth all along, and she had refused to listen. That night, after Lily was asleep, Eleanor read the opening of the Gospel of John for the first time in forty years. She wept. The Author had been standing outside the system, before it, the whole time. At her last lecture that spring, Eleanor showed her students the same slides she had always shown them. But at the end, for the first time, she told them who she believed had written the numbers, and she gave Yahweh the honor out loud.

gh-appointment-kept.title: The Extra Plate on Thursday
gh-appointment-kept.body: Every Thursday for a whole year, Mrs. Beatrice Holloway set an extra plate at her supper table. She lived alone, and her family thought it was a little odd. When her nephew asked her about it, she said only that she had been praying for a long time for a way to serve, and that during one of those prayers she had felt a quiet nudge to set a place for whoever Yahweh might send. Nobody ever came. Fifty Thursdays went by, and she washed the extra plate clean each night and put it back in the cupboard. Her friends teased her gently. But Beatrice kept setting it, because she would rather be ready and laughed at than be found unready. On the fifty-first Thursday, a terrible storm knocked out the power across the county. At a quarter past six, just as Beatrice was lighting candles, there was a knock on her door. On her porch stood a young mother with two little boys, soaked to the skin. Their car had slid into the ditch at the end of the lane, and hers was the only house with a light. Beatrice brought them inside and wrapped them in quilts. Then she looked at her table and laughed out loud. There were not enough plates, of course. But there was one extra, already set, and she pulled two more down from the cupboard in a hurry. The young mother said she had been praying in the car for somewhere to go. Beatrice said she had been praying for a year for someone to come. They both decided, over warm soup by candlelight, that this was no accident. The appointment had simply been kept.

gh-appointment-kept.title: The Window Facing the Road
gh-appointment-kept.body: When Arthur's son Michael left home in anger, Arthur was fifty. When Arthur was seventy-six, he still sat each morning in the chair by the front window that faced the road. In the early years, the waiting was full of pain. Later it became something quieter, almost holy. Arthur prayed in that chair every day, and over time he grew certain, with a certainty he could not explain to anyone, that Yahweh had promised him he would see his son again before he died. He told only his pastor. His pastor did not argue with him. He simply said that if the promise was from Yahweh, it would be kept to the letter. One autumn Arthur grew sick, and his daughter wanted him to move to her house in the city. Arthur refused. He did not know why, only that he felt he must stay in the chair by the window a little longer. His daughter thought he was being stubborn. On a bright Tuesday in October, Arthur felt an unusual pull to go out and sit on the porch instead of inside, though the morning was cold. He wrapped himself in a blanket and went. Twenty minutes later, a car he did not recognize turned into the lane. A gray-haired man got out, stood at the bottom of the steps, and could not speak. It was Michael. He had driven across three states, he said, because for a week he had not been able to stop thinking about home. Arthur held his son in his arms on the porch. He had been positioned at the very hour, and he had not missed it. That winter, Arthur went Home in peace.

gh-no-guile-figtree.title: The Treehouse Prayer
gh-no-guile-figtree.body: Nora was nine and had been chosen to pray out loud at the church picnic, and she was terrified. All week she practiced long, fancy prayers in front of her bedroom mirror, full of words she had heard grown-ups use, like "bountiful" and "beseech." She wanted everyone to think she was very spiritual. By Friday she had written three pages and could not remember any of them. On Saturday she ran to the treehouse in the backyard, the place she went when she was upset, and burst into tears. Between sobs she told the Lord the truth: she was scared, she did not know the fancy words, and she just wanted to say thank You for her family and for the picnic and for the dog. Then she climbed down, feeling a little better but still worried. That evening her grandmother found the three crumpled pages in the trash. She sat beside Nora on the bed. "I saw you up in the treehouse this afternoon," Grandma said. "I didn't hear what you said. But I'm sure He did. He saw you up there before anyone else did, and He liked that prayer just fine." Nora thought about that. If Yahweh had already seen her, crying and honest in the treehouse, then there was nobody to impress. He already knew exactly who she was. At the picnic the next day, Nora stood up in front of everyone, folded her hands, and simply said thank You for her family, for the food, for the sunshine and for the dog. It took about fifteen seconds. Several of the old men wiped their eyes. Nora did not notice. She was talking to Someone who already knew her.

gh-no-guile-figtree.title: The Mask in the Third Pew
gh-no-guile-figtree.body: Everyone at Cedar Hill Church thought Gerald was the model of a faithful man. He sat in the third pew every Sunday in a pressed suit, he taught the men's class, and he always had a cheerful word. But Gerald carried a secret. Years earlier, before he came to Cedar Hill, he had failed badly. He had walked away from his first family, and he had never told anyone. He had built a whole new life on top of that failure and covered it so carefully that sometimes he almost believed the covering himself. Even in prayer, Gerald wore the mask. He prayed the kind of prayers a model Christian would pray. He spoke to Yahweh as if Yahweh, too, might be fooled. One night, sitting alone in his car after the men's class, Gerald finally understood that the mask had never worked on the One it mattered most to hide from. Long before he walked into that church, long before he ever sat in the third pew, Yahweh had seen him. He had seen the failure and every hidden hour since, and He had still called Gerald to Himself. There was nothing to manage. There was no one to perform for. Gerald wept in the dark parking lot and told the Lord the whole truth for the first time in thirty years. In the months that followed, he wrote a letter to the children he had left, and to his surprise, one of them wrote back. He told his pastor everything. He kept teaching the men's class, but now he taught it without the mask, and the men began to tell him the truth about themselves, too. Gerald had been fully seen, and he was finally free.

gh-foreknew-betrayer.title: Mom Knew About the Cookies
gh-foreknew-betrayer.body: Every afternoon that week, Henry sneaked two chocolate chip cookies from the jar on top of the refrigerator. He waited until his mother was in the garden, dragged a chair over, climbed up, and took exactly two, so she would not notice. By Thursday he was feeling very clever. Then on Friday morning, his mother made him a big breakfast of pancakes with strawberries, his favorite, and sat down across from him with her coffee. "I know about the cookies," she said quietly. Henry nearly dropped his fork. "You knew? Since when?" "Since Monday. I counted them." Henry stared at his pancakes. "Then why didn't you stop me? And why are you making me pancakes?" His mother smiled sadly. "Because I love you, and I was waiting to see whether you'd tell me yourself." Henry thought about this. For a moment he had an idea: if Mom already knew, and she still loved him, then maybe it did not matter. Maybe he could keep doing it. His mother seemed to read his face. "Henry, my knowing doesn't make it all right. I knew what you were doing, but you're the one who chose to do it. And you're the one who gets to choose what happens now." Henry put down his fork. His face went red. Then, slowly, he told her the whole thing, every cookie, and said he was sorry. He offered to do extra chores to pay for them. His mother forgave him and hugged him over the table. Afterward Henry thought it was strange. He had felt so clever being sneaky. He felt much better being known and honest.

gh-foreknew-betrayer.title: The Apprentice at the Bench
gh-foreknew-betrayer.body: Old Matthias had been a master cabinetmaker for fifty years when he took on an apprentice named Jonah, a bright young man with quick hands and a hungry heart. Matthias gave him the best bench in the shop, by the window. He taught him to read the grain of walnut and to set a dovetail so tight that it needed no glue. He fed him lunch every day and treated him like a son. And within a few months, Matthias knew that Jonah was stealing from him. Small things at first: a chisel, a box of brass hinges, then cash from the drawer. Jonah thought no one had noticed. He told himself the old man was too trusting to see, and that even if he did, he would never send away a favorite. Matthias did see. He saw all of it. And he kept teaching Jonah, kept setting his lunch on the bench, and kept praying for him every night. One evening, as Jonah was closing up, Matthias quietly called him over and laid the stolen chisel on the bench between them. "I have known since the first week," the old man said. "I have loved you every day since. But my knowing does not make you faithful, son. That part is yours to choose, and you will answer for what you choose." Jonah stood frozen. He had believed that being loved meant he could not be held to account. Now he saw that the love had been calling him toward repentance all along, and that the time to answer was running short. Jonah broke down and confessed everything. He paid back every coin over two years. Matthias left him the shop when he died.

gh-enemy-injects-thoughts.title: Sorting the Mail
gh-enemy-injects-thoughts.body: Every day after school, Ivy helped her father sort the mail. Bills went in one pile, letters from Grandma in another, and the flyers and junk went straight into the recycling bin. "Not everything that comes to our door is ours to keep," her father liked to say. One evening Ivy came home from school very quiet. At supper she pushed her peas around her plate. Finally she said, "I keep thinking that I'm not as smart as my sister. And that nobody really likes me." Her father put down his fork. "Where did those thoughts come from?" Ivy shrugged. "They just showed up in my head. So I guess they're mine." Her father went to the counter and came back with the stack of mail. He picked up a flyer for a car sale. "This came to our house. Is it ours?" Ivy giggled. "No, it's junk." "Right. It arrived at our door, but that doesn't mean we have to sign for it. Thoughts can be like that. Some of them didn't start with you. So we do four things: notice the thought, test it against what Yahweh says about you, capture it, and redirect it to what is true." Together they did it. Ivy noticed the thought. They tested it: Yahweh made her and loved her, and her friend Maya had saved her a seat at lunch every day that week. So the thought was junk. They captured it, and Ivy pretended to drop it in the recycling bin. Then they redirected it, and she wrote one true thing on a sticky note for her mirror. After that, whenever a junk thought arrived, Ivy sorted the mail.

gh-enemy-injects-thoughts.title: The Sale of the Back Lot
gh-enemy-injects-thoughts.body: Ben and Clara Whitfield had owned a small lot behind their house for twenty years. When their church began raising money to build a shelter for families without homes, they decided to sell the lot and give the money to the building fund. They told the pastor at a meeting, and everyone applauded. The lot sold for more than they had expected. And that night, sitting at the kitchen table with the check in front of them, a thought arrived in Ben's mind as smoothly as if it had always been his. Nobody knows the price. We could give most of it, say it was all, and keep a little back for ourselves. It would still be generous. It made perfect sense. It felt like his own good idea. He started to say it out loud. Then Clara looked up at him, and something in her face made him stop. She told him later that she had felt the very same thought arrive in her own mind at the same moment, just as smooth, and that it had frightened her. It had not felt like her. It had felt like something whispering through a crack in the door. They sat together and did what their pastor had taught them: they noticed the thought, they tested it against the Word, and it failed. It was a lie dressed up as generosity. So they captured it, prayed together, and refused it. The next morning they gave the whole amount and told the truth about every dollar. Later, when they had sat with it, both of them were shaken by how close they had come. A thought had almost become a deed. It had been stopped at the door.

gh-spirits-seek-a-body.title: The Bare Garden Bed
gh-spirits-seek-a-body.body: Theo's grandmother gave him one garden bed of his own the spring he turned ten, and it was full of weeds. Theo spent a whole Saturday pulling every single one. He raked the soil smooth until it looked like brown velvet, and he swept the path around it. Then he went inside, very proud, and did nothing else with it. Two weeks later the bed was full of weeds again, thicker and taller than before, with thistles and creeping vines he had never seen. Theo could not understand it. "I cleaned it out perfectly," he complained. Grandma knelt beside him. "You did. But you left it empty. Empty ground never stays empty. If you don't plant something good, the weeds will move right back in, and they'll bring their friends." So the next Saturday Theo pulled the weeds again, and this time he planted the bed full: beans, carrots, marigolds and a row of sunflowers along the back. When the plants came up, they grew so close together that the weeds had no room. That summer Theo noticed something about himself, too. His mother had asked him to stop complaining so much, and he had tried, but the complaints kept coming back. Then his grandmother suggested he fill the space instead. So every night at bedtime, he started telling Yahweh three things he was thankful for. He found that the thankfulness took up the room where the complaints used to grow. By August, his garden bed was so full of vegetables that he gave baskets to the neighbors. His heart was fuller, too. He had learned that clearing out was only half the job.

gh-spirits-seek-a-body.title: The Empty Evenings
gh-spirits-seek-a-body.body: For fifteen years, Raymond's evenings belonged to the bottle. He was never cruel, but he was never fully present either, and his wife and children learned to tiptoe around the hours after supper. Then one New Year's Day he poured every bottle down the sink and quit. His family was overjoyed. For a few months, he stayed clean. But Raymond had only emptied the house. He had not filled it. His evenings now stretched out long and blank in front of him. He sat in front of the television with nothing to do and nothing to hold on to. The old craving prowled around the edges of those empty hours, looking for a way back in. In the fall, he lost his job, and the craving found the door open. When he fell, he fell harder than before, and it nearly cost him his marriage. It was his brother-in-law, a quiet man named Luis, who sat with him in the hospital and told him the truth plainly. "You swept the house, Ray. You never moved anyone in. You can't just stop. You have to be filled." Raymond had no idea what that meant. Luis showed him. He took him to a men's group at his church that met on Tuesday and Thursday nights, the very hours that had been empty. He read the Word with him on the phone every night at nine. Raymond asked Jesus to come and live in the house he had swept, and to fill it with His Holy Spirit. It did not happen overnight. But there was no vacancy anymore. Ten years later, Raymond leads the Tuesday night group himself, and his evenings are full.

gh-not-my-will-but-thine.title: The Moving Truck
gh-not-my-will-but-thine.body: When Sophie's father was asked by his company to move across the country, Sophie cried for three days. She was eleven. She loved her school, her best friend Mae lived next door, and she had planned to be on the swim team that spring. She prayed every night that the move would be canceled. She prayed very specifically, with details, and told Yahweh exactly how it should go. The move was not canceled. The night before the truck came, Sophie sat on the floor of her empty room, and her mother came and sat beside her. Her mother reminded her of the night Jesus prayed in the garden, and how He trusted His Father's plan above His own wish. "That's the harder half of praying," her mother said. "It isn't giving up. It's trusting Him with how it turns out." Sophie did not like that at all. But she was too tired to argue, so she prayed it anyway, the harder half. She told Yahweh she still did not want to go, but that she would go if He wanted her to, and that she would trust Him. The new town was strange at first. But in the second week, a girl named Priya sat beside her at lunch and asked if she liked to swim. The new school had a swim team too, a better one. And on Sundays, Sophie found a church youth group where she learned more about Jesus in a year than she ever had before. Mae came to visit that summer. Sophie took her to the lake, and told her that the move she had cried over had turned into a gift.

gh-not-my-will-but-thine.title: The Long Illness
gh-not-my-will-but-thine.body: When Margaret was fifty-two, she was diagnosed with an illness that the doctors said would not go away. It would not take her life quickly, but it would slowly take her strength. For the first year, she prayed fiercely to be healed. She asked for it every day, and she asked her church to ask, and she meant every word. Healing did not come. Her strength faded, as the doctors had said it would. There was a dark winter when she was angry and frightened and would not pray at all. Then one night, unable to sleep, Margaret read about the night Jesus prayed in the garden, and she saw that the King Himself had prayed both halves: He had asked for the suffering to be taken away, and then He had trusted Himself to His Father. She saw that surrender was not losing. It was trust. So Margaret began to pray the harder half. She still asked for healing. But she also told the Father that she was placing her soul in His keeping, whatever came, and that she would keep doing good as long as she had strength to do it. From her bed she wrote cards to every shut-in at her church. She prayed for the nurses by name. She taught her granddaughter to knit and told her about Jesus while their needles clicked. Her body did not prosper. But her soul did, in a way that astonished everyone who visited her. People came to cheer her up and left cheered themselves. When Margaret went Home, her pastor said that he had never seen a soul more safely kept than hers, in a body that was failing.

gh-wheat-and-tares.title: The Eager Weeder
gh-wheat-and-tares.body: Grandpa Eli let his grandson Caleb help in the wheat field the spring Caleb turned eight. Caleb was very eager. He walked between the rows and began pulling up every green shoot that looked a little different from its neighbors. He was sure he was getting rid of the weeds. He filled a whole bucket before Grandpa noticed. "Whoa there," said Grandpa, kneeling down and pulling a shoot out of the bucket. "This is wheat, Caleb. And this one too. When they're this young, the wheat and the weeds look almost the same. If you pull now, you'll tear up good wheat along with the bad." "Then what do we do with the weeds?" "We let them grow together until harvest. When it's time to bring in the wheat, the difference will be easy to see. That's when they get sorted. Not now, and not by us." Caleb looked at his bucket and felt terrible. Grandpa ruffled his hair. "Your job is just to be good wheat." That fall, Caleb started third grade, and there was a boy in his class named Rory who was always in trouble. Caleb had decided Rory was a weed. But one day he remembered the bucket in Grandpa's field, and he stopped deciding. He started sitting with Rory at lunch instead. By the end of the year, Rory had become one of his best friends, and he came to church with Caleb's family at Easter. At harvest time, Caleb stood beside Grandpa as the combine moved across the golden field, and he was glad that sorting things out was not his job. His job was to grow.

gh-wheat-and-tares.title: The Elder and the Young Man
gh-wheat-and-tares.body: Brother Samuel had been an elder at River Road Church for twenty-five years, and he believed he could spot trouble a mile away. When a young man named Devon began showing up on Sunday mornings with a hard face and a bad reputation, Samuel was certain. Devon had been in trouble with the law. He sat in the back and left before the closing hymn. Samuel told the other elders it would be best for everyone if the young man were quietly encouraged to find another church. Old Mother Ellis, who had been praying in that church for longer than Samuel had been alive, heard about it and asked to speak with him. She told him she had grown up on a farm, and that her father had taught her something about fields. You cannot always tell the good grain from the bad while it is growing. If you go pulling, you will tear up the good with the bad. The sorting belongs to the harvest, and the harvest belongs to the King. "You are not the reaper, Samuel," she said gently. "Neither am I. Our job is to be good seed in a mixed field." Samuel did not like it, but he let it go. Devon stayed. He kept sitting in the back. Then one Sunday he stayed through the closing hymn. Two years later, Devon gave his life to Jesus, and later still, he started a ministry for young men coming home from prison. Samuel was in the front row the day Devon was ordained. Afterward he found Mother Ellis and told her she had been right. He had nearly pulled up the very wheat that the King was growing.

gh-sheep-and-goats.title: The Shepherd at the County Fair
gh-sheep-and-goats.body: At the county fair, Lena and her little brother Jack watched an old shepherd named Mr. Duffy bring his flock into the show barn. The sheep and goats had been grazing together all summer in the same hills, and in the pen they all crowded in together, a wooly, bleating jumble. Then Mr. Duffy opened two gates, one on his right and one on his left, and began to separate them. He did it quickly and calmly, as if he had done it a thousand times. Sheep to the right, goats to the left. He never hesitated. Jack was amazed. "How does he know which is which so fast? Some of them look the same." Their grandmother laughed. "He's known every one of them since they were born. And besides, he says the sheep follow him and the goats mostly do what they please." On the drive home, Grandma told them that Jesus had used that very picture to describe the end of the age. For now everyone grows up together, in the same towns and schools and even churches. But one day there will be a separating, and the Shepherd will know His own. Lena was quiet for a while. "So how do you make sure you're a sheep?" she asked. Grandma thought about it. "You follow the Shepherd now. In little things. Every day. Telling the truth when it's hard. Being kind when nobody's looking. Listening for His voice. The line between sheep and goats gets walked a step at a time, long before it's drawn." That night, Lena told her brother the truth about who had broken the lamp. It was a small thing. But she felt like a sheep.

gh-sheep-and-goats.title: The Two Brothers on Elm Street
gh-sheep-and-goats.body: Frank and Eddie Morrow grew up side by side in the same house on Elm Street. They went to the same school, sat in the same pew at the same church, and heard the same sermons from the same pastor. From the outside, no one could have told them apart. But somewhere in their teenage years, they began to choose differently, one small choice at a time. Frank followed Jesus in the thousand small obediences that nobody sees: telling the truth, keeping his promises, praying when he did not feel like it, forgiving when he did not want to. Eddie went through the motions on Sunday and did as he pleased the rest of the week. He was not a wicked man. He simply never followed. He assumed there was plenty of time and that, in the end, everyone in the pew would be treated the same. When the brothers were in their sixties, Eddie had a heart attack. In the hospital, with machines beeping around him, he looked up at Frank and asked a question he had never asked. "Is it true? That there's a separating at the end?" Frank held his brother's hand and did not soften it. He told him yes, it was real and it was final, and that the two destinies did not mix. And he told him that the Shepherd was still calling, and that the gate was still open while there was breath. Eddie wept. That night, he gave his life to Jesus. He lived four more years. He spent every one of them following, in small things, as if each day mattered. He told Frank he was sorry it took him so long to start walking the line.

gh-judgment-committed-to-son.title: The Self-Appointed Hall Monitor
gh-judgment-committed-to-son.body: Grace was in fifth grade, and she had appointed herself the judge of everyone. She knew who talked in the library, who cut in the lunch line, and who copied homework, and she kept a little notebook with all their names. Every day she reported them to Mrs. Carter, her teacher, and every day she felt a little more tired and a little more angry. It was a lot of work keeping track of everybody's wrongs. One afternoon Mrs. Carter kept Grace after class. "Grace, I know you want things to be fair. But I want to tell you something. Deciding who gets in trouble isn't your job. It's mine, and the principal's. You don't have to carry that." Grace was surprised to feel relieved. She had not known she was allowed to put the notebook down. That night at dinner, she told her family about it. Her father nodded. He said that the judging of every soul has been placed in the hands of Jesus, not in ours. Every person she met, her father said, was His to judge, not hers. "So what's my job, then?" Grace asked. "To honor Him," her mother said. "And to treat people the way someone treats people who belong to Him." Grace threw the notebook away the next morning. At recess she saw a boy cut in the line for the swings, and instead of writing his name down, she just let it go. Later that week, she helped the same boy pick up the books he dropped in the hallway. She felt lighter than she had in months.

gh-judgment-committed-to-son.title: The Sister Who Held the Gavel
gh-judgment-committed-to-son.body: When their mother was dying, Rebecca's brother Paul did not come. He did not call, and he did not visit, and he did not come to the funeral. Rebecca handled everything herself: the hospital, the nursing home, the bills, the hard conversations with doctors. When it was over, she found that she had become Paul's judge. In her mind she held court every night. She laid out the evidence and pronounced the sentence. She told herself she would never speak to him again, and for three years she did not. Her heart grew heavy and hard. Her pastor noticed. One day after church he asked her a question she did not expect. "Rebecca, whose courtroom is your brother's soul in?" She had no answer. The pastor reminded her that the judging of every soul belongs to Jesus, and that honoring Him means leaving His cases in His hands. Paul was His case, he said, not hers. And the Judge, unlike her, knew everything: the whole story, every hidden thing, every reason and every wound. And He had bled for the defendants. Rebecca went home and sat in her car for a long time. She realized she had been sitting in a seat that had never been hers, and that holding court every night was exhausting her. So she gave it up. She told Jesus that Paul belonged to Him, and that she would honor His judgment instead of her own. She did not pretend it had not hurt. But she stopped holding the gavel. A year later, Paul called. He told her things about those months that she had never known. She was glad she had not been the one passing sentence.

gh-hear-believe-no-condemnation.title: The Library Fine
gh-hear-believe-no-condemnation.body: Simon was ten, and he owed the town library more money than he had ever seen in his life. He had borrowed six books about ships in the spring, lost them under his bed, and found them in October. The fine had grown every single day. When he finally carried the books back, the slip of paper the computer printed made his stomach drop. He could not pay it. Not with his allowance, not in a year. So Simon stopped going to the library. He walked the long way around it on his way home from school, so he would not have to pass the front window. He worried about it at night. He imagined the head librarian, Mrs. Abernathy, sending a letter to his parents, or calling his school. One afternoon Mrs. Abernathy was outside watering the flowers by the steps when Simon tried to sneak past. She called him by name. Simon froze. "I've been looking for you," she said. "I wanted to tell you something myself. I'm the one who decides about fines, and I cleared yours the day you brought those books back. There is nothing on your card. Nothing at all." Simon stared at her. "Really? Can I have that in writing?" She laughed. "You have my word. That's better." Simon had a choice. He could keep walking the long way around, still afraid. Or he could believe the very person who had the authority to decide. The next day he walked right through the front doors and checked out three books about trains. That night he slept like a stone, and he never walked the long way around again.

gh-hear-believe-no-condemnation.title: The Woman Who Was Afraid of the Last Day
gh-hear-believe-no-condemnation.body: Mrs. Evelyn Price was eighty-seven and had gone to church every Sunday of her life, and she was terrified of dying. She had never told anyone. But late at night she lay awake thinking about the day she would stand before the Judge, and every time she tried to picture it, she saw only her failures: the sharp words she had spoken to her sister, the years she had been too proud to apologize to her son, the hundred small sins she could not even remember. She did not know if she had been good enough. Nobody could know that, she thought. When her health began to fail, a young chaplain named Mr. Ortiz began visiting her. One afternoon she finally told him her fear. Mr. Ortiz did not argue with her. He opened his Bible to the fifth chapter of John and read aloud the words of Jesus about hearing and believing. Then he closed the book and looked at her kindly. "Mrs. Price, those are the words of the Judge Himself. The very One who will preside. He has already told you the verdict for those who believe Him. It isn't a guess. He published it. Do you believe Him?" Evelyn was quiet for a long time. She had spent so many years trying to guess what the Judge would say that she had never simply taken Him at His word. "I do," she whispered. "I believe Him." Something left her face that afternoon, and it never came back. In the last months of her life, she slept well. She talked about Home the way a person talks about a trip she is looking forward to.

gh-word-judges-last-day.title: The Rubric on the Refrigerator
gh-word-judges-last-day.body: On the first day of sixth grade, Mr. Haddad handed every student a sheet of paper. "This is the rubric for your science fair project," he said. "Everything I'll grade you on is right here. There are no surprises. And if you need help understanding any part of it, my door is open every day after school." Lucas folded the paper and stuck it in his backpack, where it stayed, crumpled and forgotten, until February. His friend Ana took hers home and taped it to her refrigerator. Every week she read it over. She went to Mr. Haddad's room twice after school with questions, and he helped her both times. When the science fair came, Ana's project was ready. Every point on the rubric was covered. Lucas threw his project together the night before and was shocked when he got his grade. "That's not fair!" he said. "I didn't know you'd grade us on all that!" Mr. Haddad gently pulled a copy of the rubric from his desk. "Lucas, I gave this to you on the very first day. I offered to help you every afternoon. The standard was never a secret." Lucas looked at the paper and turned red. He knew it was true. That night, Lucas told his father about it. His father was quiet a moment, then said that this was how the Word works too. The standard every person will be measured by at the end has already been given, plainly, with mercy offered first. "Nobody gets ambushed," he said. "But you have to read it." The next morning, Lucas taped his rubric to his bedroom wall. And beside it, he put a Bible.

gh-word-judges-last-day.title: The Father Who Read at Night
gh-word-judges-last-day.body: Every night for twenty years, after supper, Joseph Mensah read the Word aloud to his children at the kitchen table. When they were small, they sat in his lap. When they were teenagers, they rolled their eyes. He read anyway. His neighbor Bill, leaning on the fence one evening, asked him why he bothered. "Kids today won't listen to that. Besides, nobody really knows what Yahweh is going to judge us by at the end. Everybody has an opinion." Joseph set down his rake. "I don't think it's a secret, Bill. It's already written down. It's sitting on my kitchen table. Jesus came with mercy first, and He left His words with us ahead of time, so nobody would be surprised." Bill did not say anything. He went back inside. Years later, Joseph's youngest son, Kofi, went through a hard season. He drifted far from home and far from faith, and for a long time he wanted nothing to do with any of it. But one night, alone in a strange city, he found a Bible in a hotel drawer, and as he turned the pages he realized he knew them. He had heard nearly every one of them at his father's table, night after night, when he thought he was not listening. The words were the same words. And he knew what they asked of him, because he had been given them for twenty years. Kofi called home the next morning. When Bill heard about it, he asked Joseph if he would read with his grandchildren too.

gh-thief-targets-identity.title: The Birdhouse
gh-thief-targets-identity.body: For most of third grade, Owen believed he was stupid. It started with one boy on the playground who said it, and then another, and then it became a voice in Owen's own head whenever he tried something new. You're not good at this. Don't even try. By spring he had stopped raising his hand in class and had stopped building things in the garage with his grandfather, which he used to love more than anything. Grandpa Ike noticed. One Saturday he brought Owen into the garage and set a pile of cedar boards on the workbench. "Help me make a birdhouse." "I'm not good at building," Owen mumbled. Grandpa put down his hammer. "Who told you that?" Owen shrugged. "Owen, listen to me. Yahweh made you. He made your hands and your brain and your imagination, on purpose. He's the only One who knows everything you can do. Anybody who tells you different is trying to steal something that doesn't belong to them." Owen looked at his hands. Grandpa handed him a pencil and a ruler. It took all afternoon, and Owen made mistakes. But by suppertime there was a birdhouse on the bench, crooked roof and all, and Owen had built most of it himself. Before they hung it in the oak tree, Grandpa had him carve something on the bottom. Owen thought about it, then carved in careful letters: Yahweh made me able. That spring, a pair of bluebirds moved in. Owen started raising his hand again. And whenever the old voice came back, he thought about the letters on the bottom of the birdhouse, and he knew whose credit it really was.

gh-thief-targets-identity.title: What Was Taken in the Layoff
gh-thief-targets-identity.body: For twenty-three years, Diane had been the head nurse on the night shift at the county hospital. She was good at it. The younger nurses came to her with every hard case, and patients asked for her by name. Then the hospital merged with a bigger system, and on a Tuesday afternoon she was called into an office and told her position no longer existed. She went home and sat at her kitchen table in her uniform until dark. In the weeks that followed, something worse than the job loss crept in. A steady, quiet voice told her she had never been as good as she thought. That she was old and useless. That her whole life had been a mistake. She stopped going to church. She stopped calling her friends. She stopped praying, because she was no longer sure who she was praying as. Her sister Ruth drove up from the city and found her like that. Ruth listened, and then she said something Diane never forgot. "Diane, you're being robbed. That voice isn't telling you the truth about who you are. It's trying to steal what Yahweh put in you, your skill, your care, your calling, and to make sure He never gets thanked for any of it." Diane cried for a long time. Then she let Ruth pray with her. Slowly, she began to give the credit back to the One who had made her, out loud, every morning. Six months later, she started a small clinic in the basement of her church, caring for people without insurance. She told everyone who asked that the skill in her hands had never been hers to lose. It had been given, and she was giving it back.

gh-pray-for-protection.title: The Cookie Jar on the High Shelf
gh-pray-for-protection.body: Wesley had a problem with the cookie jar. His mother had told him he could have two cookies after school, and only two, but every afternoon he ended up eating five or six. He did not mean to. He just walked past the counter, and the jar was right there, and before he knew it his hand was in it. At bedtime one night he told his mother about it, feeling ashamed. His mother sat on the edge of his bed. "Do you want help?" she asked. Wesley nodded. "Then let's do two things. First, let's pray. Jesus taught us to pray for protection. So let's ask Him for that." They prayed together. Wesley asked Yahweh to help him not want so many cookies, and to keep him from being tempted. "Now the second thing," said his mother. "Praying is asking for a guard. But we have to keep watch, too. Where is the jar?" "On the counter by the door." "So you walk right past it every day. What should we do?" Wesley thought hard. "Put it somewhere I don't walk past." So they got up and moved the cookie jar to the high shelf in the pantry, behind the flour, where Wesley would have to go looking for it on purpose. The next afternoon, Wesley came home and walked straight past the empty counter. He did not even think about the cookies until his mother handed him two of them at the table. He grinned. He had prayed for help, and he had kept watch. Between the two, it had worked.

gh-pray-for-protection.title: The Hotel on the Business Trip
gh-pray-for-protection.body: Martin traveled for his work three weeks out of every month. He loved his wife and his daughters, and he loved the Lord, but he knew himself well enough to know that the long evenings alone in strange cities were dangerous for him. Loneliness and boredom were a bad pair. Years earlier, on a trip like this, he had made choices that nearly cost him his marriage. He and his wife had rebuilt their trust slowly, and Martin did not intend to lose it again. So every morning, before leaving his hotel room, he knelt by the bed and prayed the prayer Jesus taught, asking the Father to guard him that day, and he meant every word. But Martin had also learned that praying for a guard was only half of it. The other half was keeping watch. So he set rules for himself. He did not go to the hotel bar with clients after dinner, even when they teased him. He kept his evenings full: a walk, a call home, an hour with the Word, a book. He told his wife the name of every hotel and called her every night before bed. He asked a friend from church to text him on travel nights and ask how he was doing, and he answered honestly. One night in a city far from home, a situation came up that would have been easy to fall into. Martin felt the old pull. But he was sober, and alert, and he had already decided. He said goodnight and went up to his room and called his wife. He thanked Yahweh on his knees that night. The guard had held, because he had asked for it, and kept it.

gh-see-father-in-son.title: Just Like Grandpa
gh-see-father-in-son.body: Lily had worked in her Uncle Ray's bicycle shop every summer since she was nine, and now she was twelve. She knew how to patch a tube, true a wheel, and adjust brakes so they stopped smooth. She also knew that the shop had been started by her grandfather, who died before she was born, and she always wished she could have met him. One July afternoon, while they were fixing a little girl's bike for free, Lily sighed. "I wish I knew what Grandpa was like." Uncle Ray put down his wrench and laughed. "Lily, you've been watching me for three summers. I'm practically him. I talk like him. I fix bikes for free like him. Everything I know about running this shop, about treating people, I learned by watching him. If you want to know what he was like, look at me." Lily blinked. She had been standing right next to the answer the whole time and never noticed. That night she told her mother the story. Her mother smiled and said it reminded her of something. One of Jesus' closest friends had once asked Him to show them the Father, even though he had walked beside Jesus for years. And the answer had been standing right in front of him the whole time. "You can be close to something for a long time and still not see it," her mother said. "That's why we keep looking." The next Sunday, when Lily read about Jesus in the Gospels, she read it differently. Every time He healed someone, or forgave someone, or stopped for a child, she thought: this is what Yahweh is like. She had been looking right at Him.

gh-see-father-in-son.title: Forty Years in the Pew
gh-see-father-in-son.body: Martha Greer had been a member of First Street Church for forty years. She had taught Sunday school, served on every committee, cooked for every funeral and knew more hymns by heart than the choir director. And one night, at seventy-one, sitting alone in her kitchen after her husband's funeral, she realized with a shock that she did not know who Yahweh was. She knew about Him. She had heard sermons about Him for four decades. But in her grief she felt that He was a distant, faceless power, and she could not picture Him at all. She was ashamed to admit it, even to herself. Forty years, and she still did not know. The next week, she went to her pastor, a young man less than half her age, and told him the truth. She expected him to be shocked. Instead he simply opened his Bible to the Gospel of John, to the night one of Jesus' own disciples asked to be shown the Father, and he told her that the answer had been standing in front of that disciple the whole time. "Mrs. Greer, if you want to see the Father, look at the face of Jesus. Look at how He touched lepers, how He wept at His friend's tomb, how He forgave the men who crucified Him. That is what the Father is like. He's not faceless. He has a face." Martha went home and read the Gospels slowly, from the beginning, as if for the first time. And it was as if for the first time. The revelation she had sat near for forty years finally landed. She told her Sunday school class about it, humbly, and they all started reading together.

gh-he-already-knew.title: How Will We Feed Them?
gh-he-already-knew.body: Twenty minutes before supper on Saturday, the doorbell rang, and there stood Uncle Pete, Aunt Marie and their five children, smiling and holding a bag of dinner rolls. They had driven up as a surprise. Ten-year-old Abby stood in the kitchen doorway looking at the one small pot of chili on the stove. It was meant for four people. Now there were eleven. Her father came into the kitchen and looked at her very seriously. "Abby, how are we going to feed all these people?" Abby panicked. She did the math in her head. There was not enough chili. There was not enough of anything. She started listing ideas out loud: they could make smaller bowls, they could skip dessert, maybe she did not have to eat. Her father let her talk for a while. Then he smiled and opened the freezer. It was full. There were two more containers of chili, a pan of cornbread, and a whole tub of ice cream. "I bought extra when Pete called on Tuesday," he said. "I already knew what I was going to do." Abby stared at him. "Then why did you ask me?" "I wanted to see what you'd do. You went straight to counting what we didn't have. Next time, maybe start by trusting that there's a plan." At church the next morning, the teacher read about the day Jesus fed five thousand people, and the question He asked one of His disciples first. Abby nearly laughed out loud. She raised her hand and told the whole class about the freezer. She said she was going to try trusting first.

gh-he-already-knew.title: The Question in the Empty Office
gh-he-already-knew.body: When the factory closed, Leon lost the job he had held for twenty-six years. He had a wife, two children in high school and a mortgage. The first night, he sat at his desk with a calculator and a legal pad and added up everything they had and everything they owed. The numbers did not work. No matter how many times he ran them, they did not work. In the weeks that followed, Leon prayed every night, but his prayers were really just more math. He told Yahweh the numbers and asked Him to fix them. And one night, sitting in the dark, Leon felt as though the question had been turned around and handed back to him. How will you provide? It was not an accusation. It felt more like a test. Leon answered the only way he knew: with the calculator. He could not do it. Two hundred dollars a week was not enough. He was not enough. Then he remembered a sermon his pastor had preached about the day Jesus asked Philip how they would feed the crowd, and how the question had been a test from One who already had the answer. Leon put down the calculator. He realized that the One asking had never been confused about the answer. The question was not meant to stump Him. It was meant to grow Leon. So he answered differently. He told the Lord that he did not know how, but that he trusted Him to provide, and he would do the next right thing each day. Within the year, Leon was running a small repair business out of his garage. It paid better than the factory had. He kept the calculator on the shelf as a reminder.

gh-strengthen-your-brethren.title: The Bicycle Teacher
gh-strengthen-your-brethren.body: It took Hazel all summer to learn to ride her bicycle without training wheels. She fell in the driveway, in the grass, and once, spectacularly, into Mrs. Kowalski's hedge. Her knees were covered in bandages. More than once she cried and said she was never getting on that bike again. But her father kept running beside her, holding the back of the seat, telling her she could do it. And one evening in August, he let go without telling her, and Hazel rode all the way to the end of the block by herself. She was so proud she could hardly sleep. The next morning, Hazel's little cousin Felix came to visit. He was six, and he had a brand-new bicycle with training wheels, and he was terrified to take them off. Hazel watched him wobble down the sidewalk, and she remembered exactly how that felt: the fear, the falling, the hedge. She did not go off and ride on her own. She asked her uncle for a wrench. Then she spent the whole afternoon running beside Felix, holding the back of his seat, telling him he could do it. When he fell, she showed him her bandaged knees and told him she had fallen a hundred times. By the end of the week, Felix was riding on his own. That night, Hazel's father told her about the night Jesus prayed for Peter before his hardest test, and what He told Peter to do once he came through it. "Learning something hard isn't only for you," her father said. "It's so you can help the next person through it." Hazel thought about that. Then she asked if Felix's little sister had a bike yet.

gh-strengthen-your-brethren.title: The Man Who Had Fallen
gh-strengthen-your-brethren.body: For fifteen years, Dennis had been the strongest man in his church's men's group, the one everyone leaned on. Then, in a single terrible year, he failed. He lost his temper and his job. He started drinking again after a decade sober. He stopped coming to church, and he told the men who called him that he did not believe any of it anymore. He was ashamed beyond words. But Dennis had a friend named Gil who did not stop calling. Gil told him, every week, that he was praying for him to hold on, and that he was waiting for him to come home. One winter night, Dennis came home. He knelt in Gil's living room and wept and gave his life back to Jesus. The road back was slow. It took two years to rebuild what he had broken. And when he was standing again, Dennis felt the Lord press something on his heart. The growth was not for him to keep. So Dennis began to look for men who were standing where he had stood. He found them in the church parking lot, too ashamed to come in. He found them in the recovery meeting where he went every Thursday. He found them at the factory where he worked now. He did not lecture them. He told them the truth about his own fall and how he had been carried back. He prayed for them by name, the way Gil had prayed for him. Within a few years, Dennis was leading a group of twenty men, most of whom had once been where he had been. He said the worst year of his life had become the most useful thing he owned.

gh-glory-refused-or-taken.title: The Science Fair Trophy
gh-glory-refused-or-taken.body: When Jonah won first place at the state science fair for his water filter made from sand, charcoal and an old soda bottle, his school threw a little party in the cafeteria. The principal made a speech. The local paper sent a photographer. Everyone kept slapping him on the back and telling him he was a genius. Jonah liked it. He liked it a lot, maybe a little too much. By the end of the party, he had started to believe he really was a genius, smarter than everybody else in the room. Then his grandmother, who had driven two hours to be there, hugged him and whispered in his ear: "Who gave you that brain, Jonah?" Jonah thought about it on the drive home. He had worked hard on the filter, that was true. He had stayed up late and failed a dozen times. It was honest to say thank you when people congratulated him for that. But he had not made his own mind. He had not invented the way sand and charcoal clean water. He had only discovered something Yahweh had already built into the world. The next day, the paper called to ask Jonah a few questions for their article. When they asked him how he had come up with such a clever idea, Jonah said thank you, and he thanked his science teacher and his grandmother. Then he said that the real credit for how water gets clean belonged to Yahweh, who made it work that way in the first place, and that he had just been lucky enough to notice. The article printed it. His grandmother cut it out and put it on her refrigerator.

gh-glory-refused-or-taken.title: The Plaque on the Tower
gh-glory-refused-or-taken.body: Richard Vance had built half of the skyline in his city. Office towers, shopping centers, a stadium. He started with nothing and built it all himself, or so he said in every interview. When his tallest tower was finished, he had a bronze plaque made for the lobby, with his own face carved on it, and a line about the vision and genius of one man. At the dedication, the crowd applauded and the mayor praised him, and Richard soaked it in. He did not thank anyone. He certainly did not thank Yahweh. He believed he had done it all by the strength of his own hands. Within two years, it was gone. An economic collapse took his company. Then his health failed, and for a long, dark season, his mind seemed to fail with it. He lost his memory of whole weeks. He could not work. He sat in a small apartment and stared at the walls. It was his old secretary, a quiet woman named Mrs. Patel, who visited him there and read to him from the Word. Slowly, over many months, Richard came back to himself. And when he did, he saw what he had done. He had taken glory that had never belonged to him. He had been given strength, opportunity, and a gift for building, and he had stamped his own face on all of it. One evening Richard knelt on the apartment floor and gave Yahweh the honor he had withheld for forty years. He praised Him out loud. He recovered enough to work again in a small way. And when he spoke at business schools, he always told students that the most dangerous moment in a builder's life is the applause.

gh-before-abraham-i-am.title: The Book Report
gh-before-abraham-i-am.body: For her eighth-grade history class, Ruby was writing a report on great teachers of the ancient world. She had picked several: a Greek philosopher, a Chinese sage, and Jesus. Her plan was to say that all of them were wise men who taught people to be kind. It seemed like a fair and simple way to put it. To do her research, she sat down with her grandmother's old Bible and read the Gospel of John, all the way through, because it was the one her grandmother liked best. Halfway through, in the eighth chapter, Ruby stopped. She read one passage three times. Jesus was talking with a crowd about Abraham, who had lived about two thousand years earlier. And He did not say that He had lived back then. He spoke of Himself in the present tense, using the very Name Yahweh had given at the burning bush. The crowd understood exactly what He meant, because they picked up stones. Ruby put the Bible down and stared at the ceiling. This was not how a kind philosopher talked. A wise teacher might say many good things, but he would never claim to be Yahweh. Either Jesus was not good at all, or He was much more than a teacher. There was no middle choice. He had closed it Himself. Ruby went to find her grandmother, who was in the kitchen snapping beans. They talked for a long time. The next week, Ruby rewrote her report. She still wrote about the philosopher and the sage. But in the section about Jesus, she explained why He did not belong on the same list.

gh-before-abraham-i-am.title: The Admirer
gh-before-abraham-i-am.body: For most of his life, Professor Alan Whitmore had admired Jesus. He said so often. He taught a popular university course on the great moral teachers of history, and Jesus always got the longest lecture. Alan praised His kindness to the poor, His courage, His stories. He believed Jesus was one of the finest human beings who had ever lived. But only a human being. A good teacher, nothing more. In his last year before retiring, one of his students, a quiet young woman named Esther, stayed after class. She asked him, very politely, how he made sense of what Jesus said about Himself in the eighth chapter of John. Alan smiled and said he would look at it again. That night, at his desk, he did. He read the passage slowly in the original Greek. He knew that language better than almost anyone. And he saw that Jesus had not said He existed before Abraham in the past tense. He had used the present tense. He had taken the Name Yahweh gave at the burning bush and put it on His own lips, and the crowd understood exactly what He was claiming. Alan sat back in his chair. For forty years he had held Jesus as a good teacher. But a good teacher could not say that and still be good, unless it was true. Jesus had closed that door Himself. Alan did not sleep that night. Before dawn, he knelt by his desk for the first time in his life and said, simply, my Lord. At his final lecture that spring, he told his students what he had found. Esther was in the front row, crying.

gh-name-that-saves.title: What Does Your Name Mean?
gh-name-that-saves.body: In Mrs. Ramirez's fourth-grade class, the assignment was to find out what your name meant and why your parents chose it. Leo's name meant lion, which he thought was very cool. Grace's name meant kindness given freely. A boy named Felix found out his meant lucky, and he immediately bet everyone he would win the next spelling bee. On the last day of the project, a quiet girl named Hope raised her hand. She asked if she could share one more name, even though it was not hers. Mrs. Ramirez said yes. Hope stood up. "My grandpa told me about it. Before Jesus was born, an angel told Joseph what to name Him. He didn't get to choose. And the name was picked because of what He would do. It means Yahweh saves. That's the whole job, right there in the name." The class was quiet for a second. Felix asked, "So His name is like a promise?" Hope thought about it. "My grandpa says it's more than a promise. It's the promise and then the thing actually happening. Most names just say what your parents hope. His name said what He would do, and then He did it." Mrs. Ramirez smiled and wrote the name on the board with the others. After school, Leo walked home with Hope and asked her more about it. That night, Leo told his mother that he liked being named after a lion. But he said the best name he had heard all week was the one that meant Yahweh saves, because it was the only one in the whole class that had already come true.

gh-name-that-saves.title: The Waiting Room
gh-name-that-saves.body: It was three in the morning, and Carlos was alone in the hospital waiting room. His teenage son had been in a car accident. The doctors had taken him back hours ago, and nobody would tell Carlos anything. He had never been a praying man. Over the years he had tried many things to find peace: self-help books, a meditation app, long talks with a counselor, a weekend retreat in the mountains. Each one had helped a little, for a while. None of them were any help to him now. His hands were shaking. He did not know what to say or who to say it to. Then he remembered his mother. When he was a boy and frightened, she would hold him and say only one word, over and over, quietly: the name of Jesus. She never explained it. She just said the Name. Carlos had forgotten it for thirty years. Now he put his face in his hands, in the empty waiting room, and said it. Just the Name. Then he said it again. He did not know how to pray properly, so he simply asked Jesus to save his son, and to save him. Something happened in that room that Carlos could never fully explain. The shaking stopped. A peace came over him, deeper than anything any of his books had ever given him. He felt that he had finally found what he had been searching for, and there was nothing further to look for. At dawn the doctor came out. His son would recover. Months later, Carlos was baptized with his son beside him. He told the church that he had spent years looking for peace, and that it had been in a Name all along.

gh-all-power-is-his.title: The Crossing Guard
gh-all-power-is-his.body: Mrs. Pham was the smallest grown-up Daniel had ever seen. She was shorter than most fifth graders, and she had to stand on her tiptoes to reach the top shelf in the school library. So the first time Daniel saw her working as the crossing guard on Oak Street, he was worried for her. Oak Street had big trucks and buses, and some of the drivers went much too fast. Then a huge delivery truck came rumbling down the hill, and Mrs. Pham stepped calmly into the street and held up her bright red stop sign. The truck stopped. The bus behind it stopped. Every car on Oak Street stopped. And Mrs. Pham waved Daniel and his friends across, smiling, without ever raising her voice. Daniel asked her about it the next day. "How do you make the trucks stop? You're so little." Mrs. Pham laughed. "It's not me, honey. It's the sign, and the city that gave it to me. The authority isn't mine. It's just given to me to use. All I have to do is stand there and hold it up." That evening, Daniel told his father. His father said that was a lot like how believers carry the authority of Jesus. The power is all His, and He hands authority to His people to use in His name. "You don't have to be strong enough on your own," his father said. "You just stand in His name." A few weeks later, Daniel woke up from a nightmare, frightened. He remembered Mrs. Pham. He did not try to be brave on his own. He just prayed quietly in Jesus' name, and he was calm again, and he fell back asleep.

gh-all-power-is-his.title: The Young Minister Who Strained
gh-all-power-is-his.body: When Elijah Barnes became an associate pastor at twenty-six, he was determined to be powerful in prayer. He had heard stories of old saints who prayed and saw lives changed, and he wanted that. So he strained for it. He fasted until he was dizzy, he prayed until his voice was hoarse, and when he prayed over hurting people, he shouted and pleaded and worked himself up, as if the power depended on how hard he pushed. And he was exhausted and anxious all the time. Every time he prayed for someone and nothing seemed to happen, he believed he simply had not been strong enough. One afternoon he was called to the home of a family whose teenage daughter was tormented by fear. Elijah arrived already panicking. On the porch he met old Deacon Miller, who had been praying with families like this for fifty years. The old man looked at him and put a hand on his shoulder. "Son, you look like a man trying to lift a truck by himself. Whose power do you think this is?" Elijah did not know what to say. "Every bit of this power belongs to Jesus," the deacon said gently. "He gave us His authority to use in His name. You don't have to build it up. You only have to stand in what He already gave you." They went inside together. The deacon did not shout. He sat with the girl and her parents, opened the Word, and prayed quietly in the name of Jesus. A deep calm settled over that house. Elijah watched, and something settled in him too. He had been straining for something he already carried. From that day on, he prayed quietly.

gh-without-me-nothing.title: The Proud Garden Hose
gh-without-me-nothing.body: Every summer evening, eight-year-old Benny was in charge of watering his grandmother's tomatoes. He took the green hose from beside the porch, turned the spigot, and sprayed the plants until the dirt was dark and shiny. By July the tomatoes were enormous, and the neighbors stopped by to admire them. Benny began to feel very proud. "I grew those," he told his friend Marcus. "Me and my hose." One evening, he got an idea. The spigot was all the way at the back of the house, and he had to drag the hose around every time. So he unscrewed the hose from the spigot, carried it to the front garden, pointed it at the tomatoes, and squeezed the nozzle. Nothing happened. He squeezed harder. Not a drop. He shook it. He blew into it. He gave it a stern talking-to. Nothing. His grandmother came out on the porch and laughed so hard she had to sit down. "Benny, the hose doesn't make water. It just carries it. All the water comes from the spigot. The minute you unhook it, it's just a green tube." Benny turned red. Then he laughed too. That Sunday, he had to say a memory verse in front of the whole church, and he was nervous. Before he went up, his grandmother squeezed his hand and whispered, "Remember the hose." Benny closed his eyes and prayed. He asked Jesus to help him, because he could not do it without Him. Then he walked up and said his verse without a single mistake. Afterward his grandmother hugged him. Benny said he had stayed hooked up to the spigot.

gh-without-me-nothing.title: The Woman People Came To
gh-without-me-nothing.body: Sister Loretta had been praying for the sick in her small church for thirty years, and many people believed that her prayers worked. People traveled from other towns to ask her to pray for them. Some called her a healer. At first she corrected them gently. Over time, she stopped correcting them. She began to enjoy it. Little by little, without ever deciding to, she started to think of the gift as hers. She spent less time alone with the Lord, because she was busy praying for others. She read the Word less, because she felt she already knew it. She stopped asking Him what to pray, because she felt she already knew that, too. Then a young mother came to her with a son who was very sick, and Sister Loretta prayed over him with all her confidence, the way she always did. Nothing happened. Her words felt empty, like a bucket lowered into a dry well. That night, alone in her bedroom, she understood. She had become a branch that thought it was the vine. She had been measuring her life by her output, and somewhere along the way she had unplugged from the very One the output came from. She wept and asked the Lord to forgive her. In the weeks that followed, she went back to the beginning. She spent her mornings alone with Him again. She told everyone who called her a healer that she was nothing but a branch, and that every good thing came through her, not from her. The next time the young mother came, Loretta prayed with her humbly, simply, in the name of Jesus. The boy recovered. She gave Jesus all the credit, and meant it.
